a week and for the defence of Canada, a regiment composed mostly of lumberjacks, farmhands and day labourers. I mentioned the fact that all those men would be in excellent physical condition and besides that, nearly all of them would have been familiar with the handling of a gun. I added that if every member did the same, we would have in a very short period of time an army of 245,000 fresh recruits of the best kind.
The remarks of the chief, which appear at page 922 of Hansard (last line of first column and first lines of the second one), honoured me by mentioning in the house what I had said at a caucus, but at the same time I was deeply disappointed as I happened to be the one he referred to on that occasion. Here is the text of his remarks:
"An lion, member on this side of the house made the statement publicly this morning that he felt he could go into his constituency and, by making it known to his constituents that this measure had to do with the protection of Canada and our own Canadian soil, bring forward in a very short time men from the forests, from the fields and from the factories, all prepared immediately to join the Canadian forces to resist any possible invasion, and that he would be prepared to guarantee that that could be done in constituency after constituency throughout the country, once it was understood that there was the necessity of defending our own Canadian shores. I pointed out to him that in doing that he might be making the greatest mistake possible with respect to the national interest; that, to win this war, we might wish to keep at work in the forests the men who are now working in the forests, to provide the timber which will be required for docks and wharves and required immediately; that the men who are working in the factories may be a thousand times more useful to the government of this country in giving their skilled labour to the manufacture of aircraft, munitions, or other weapons of war than they could possibly be in lining up and presenting themselves for military service; equally that on the farms, if we are to perform what will be expected of us, we shall need all the production that can be effectively and rapidly carried out on the farms of our country."
It was undoubtedly because my offer was turned down by the Prime Minister eleven months ago that no other member made a similar one until you did it yourself a few days ago.
After the chief had told me in very definite terms that "I might be making the greatest mistake^ possible with respect to the national interest" if I did some recruiting in my constituency, that very statement and the wide publicity given to it made it impossible for me as well as for any other member of parliament to do any recruiting in his constituency.
At that time the government had already announced their policy about conscription. In fact it was the day before that the Prime Minister had presented a resolution for mobilization of human and material resources in the present war. I wonder if it was precisely because of that new policy of conscription that members of^ parliament were prevented from doing recruiting on a voluntary basis, which would have shown that conscription was unnecessary to recruit as large an army as could be equipped and maintained for the defence of this country but, in spite of the rebuke that I received and which was evidently
fMr. Pouliot.l
inspired by the brass hats of the war departments because it was much stronger in the afternoon than in the morning, I did not remain inactive and I did my best to assist all those who expressed to me by writing or verbally their desire to enlist into the militia, the navy or the air force.
The policy of the war departments as put into effect by those who were in contact with the people was to give the least possible chance to those who were willing to enlist.
I cannot mention all eases, but I sent you copy of a correspondence of Antoine Lagace, of Riviere-du-Loup, who has done some military service and who has written to three commanders for enlisting into the home guard: he was turned down because he was not a veteran of the first great war.
Another man, in a similar case, could enlist only because his brother-in-law was a sergeant, and it was considered something like a government favour to be accepted in the army.
I insist on that; it was considered a government favour to be accepted in the army.
How many men wanted to enlist as truck drivers, and how many were accepted?
I have mentioned in the house the difficulties that our boys had with regard to medical examination. Many difficulties have arisen from the fact that those who were unfit were accepted and those who were really fit were declared unfit. Finally, since the establishment of conscription, some who desired to enlist had to travel at their own expenses from Riviere-du-Loup to Quebec city and if they were declared unfit by your medical staff, they had to pay their travelling expenses from their own pockets.
Whatever could have been the intention of the government in the application of the mobilization act, in my constituency, I had the impression that everything was done not to recruit the best army, but to justify the uncalled for policy of conscription.
Please find herewith enclosed copy of letter which I am sending to-day to your colleague, the Hon. Minister of National Defence for Air. It is from Jean-Joseph Lajoie, who has a brother in the air force and another one in the navy. He says that he is so anxious to enlist in the Royal Canadian Air Force that, although he knows English very little, he is ready to spend the money that he has to learn it. I presume that he will have no opportunity to get there, although I am sure that he would do very well because that career appeals to him. I also enclose another letter to the same effect which I received to-day from L. Paul Ouellet, of Riviere-du-Loup station. It speaks by itself.
That man has been taken in.
My first cousin, Yves Bertrand, had won medals as an athlete and a marksman. Squadron-leader Stewart could tell you the trouble I had to have him enlisted as a gunner and it is only thanks to Mr. Stewart's intervention that he could get in.
Now-, regarding the manufactures of munitions, you could be astounded in reading the letter from Donat Champagne, a settler of St. Elzear, in the back country of my constituency. I wonder if it would not be possible to secure work for .him although he is a mechanic of great experience.
By the way, three people in the employment office in Quebec have been arrested because

Supply-National Defence
they were selling jobs, and no one could get in unless he paid something to the people higher up. This explains why we have trouble. I mentioned the matter a long time ago to some people, but I never succeeded in getting anywhere until those people were arrested. I continue with the letter:
Sometimes, you may find that I am grouchy and of unpleasant disposition: there is always a reason for it and I will give some of them.
Before the war, I recommended more boys for the air services than any other member ever did. General Lafleehe could tell you about it, and he was satisfied with those boys amongst whom was a nephew of your colleague, Right Honourable Mr. Lapointe. But now, since the war started, it seems as if French-Canadians were unwelcome in the army, in the navy and in the air force, and the first thing to do would be to remove all barriers seen or unseen, and, in the latter ease, badly felt, which prevent French-speaking Canadians from enlisting when they are perfectly willing to do so.
In the first place, the medical examiners shall be competent and unbiased; they shall be thoroughly familiar with French language and easily accessible, which means that no one would have to pay travelling expenses to undergo medical examination which will establish definitely and to the satisfaction of the recruit whether he is fit or not.
In the second place, the French-speaking Canadians shall be under French-speaking officers and the men shall be in a position to expect and to receive legitimate promotions in due course. On this point, I will quote the case of Sergeant Major Leo Pinel who has been in the army for several years, had won all the cups and trophies of his regiment, and has been on guard at Buckingham Palace. Colonel DesRosiers could tell you about it, as I took up this case unsuccessfully with him.
I do not blame Colonel DesRosiers; he just placed my letter before general headquarters overseas. It continues:
That fellow is very popular in a certain part of my constituency. In fact, on the occasion of the opening of a new post office at Cabano, where his family lives, I paid a tribute to him as a sportsman and a soldier, adding that on account of his services it was expected that he would soon get the promotion he was entitled to in the army. At that point, there were prolonged cheers from the whole crowd. You will understand that if Pinel gets a well-deserved promotion it will have a very good effect for increasing voluntary enlistment where he is so favourably known.
What astonishes me is the considerable number of French-Canadians who have already enlisted in spite of so many obstacles to overcome.
It is bad for a man who is ready to enlist to have a door slammed in his face. He is not anxious to go back. The letter continues:
It is true that the members of parliament are more familiar with the feelings of the people because they are in daily contact with them, but if they convey to you suggestions that really originated from the people, what-14873-249*
ever it is, you pay no attention to it and you seem to prefer to listen to the so-called military experts that Hore-Belisha has expelled from the war office.
I wonder if you ever realized that the success of voluntary enlistment in this war is largely due not to any public speeches, but to the painstaking efforts of the members of parliament who are spending lots of time with their people trying to explain and make as acceptable as possible policies for which they have never been consulted.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend
sent me the letter to which he has referred, enclosing the memorandum-or a previous letter, I have forgotten which it was. As he understands, I could not go into a long and detailed correspondence in connection with the various matters indicated in the letter. But I did, as a matter of fact, make inquiries about.it.
His first letter has to do with a statement made by the Prime Minister in the House of Commons with regard to the relative benefits of recruiting, and of the calling up of men under the National Resources Mobilization Act. If hon. members will refer to the passage in question I am sure they will realize at once that the Prime Minister was endeavouring to indicate that under the National Resources Mobilization Act provision was made for the postponement of those in essential industries. That, I believe, was what was meant by the Prime Minister's statement, and I do not feel that it would be a justification for my hon. friend's feeling that he could not take part in a recruiting campaign and in asking men to enlist.
The other part is more important, so far as I am concerned. It has to do with the welcoming of French-Canadians to the Canadian Army. May I say to the hon. member for Temiscouata-and this is no idle statement, no platitude-that I do not think any matter of policy has received more intensive attention from me than has that same matter. And I can say to my hon. friend that I have tried day in and day out, avowedly

I have made no secret of it-to see to it that just as far as possible our friends in French Canada are represented in the army, and are represented in as high places as they could possibly fill.
As a matter of fact Brigadier Archambault was recommened for a brigade in the third division, since I have been Minister of National Defence. Brigadier Reynaud has been made deputy quartermaster general. Brigadier Leclere was given a brigade overseas. He has just been returned as being medically unfit. I may point out further that a number of staff appointments have been made.
Supply

National Defence

I must say to my hon. friend and to the house and country generally that instructions at National Defence headquarters are that every effort should be made to see that French-Canadians have fair representation in appointments. There is no reason for not doing so; that is part of the national effort. It is part of the effort for the unity of Canada. I make no apology for taking that stand, and I believe hon. members of the committee will concur with me in the stand I have taken.
There are difficulties of course, and my hon. friend has pointed them out. One difficulty is connected with the question of language. I take the position that there are two official languages in this country, and that a man is entitled to speak French and to say, "That is all I can speak," just as a man is entitled to speak English, and to say, "That is all I can speak." May I pay this tribute, to the French-Canadians, that there are far more French-Canadians than there are English who are bilingual-yes, far more.
The situation with regard to enlistments and appointments is this, that in connection with units other than infantry units a man who does not speak English finds difficulty. It is difficult for a man to hold a position of command or responsibility in those other units. In fact, it is difficult for a man in those units to carry on, unless he does understand English. The technical terms in connection with the artillery, signals, ordnance and army service corps is in English. It is therefore difficult to have all French-Canadian units in those particular services. But we are trying to meet the situation in two ways. We are having French-Canadian units as far as we can, and I want to pay my tribute to those units which I saw overseas representing the province of Quebec. They were fine units, wholly French-Canadian, and officered by French-Canadians. They have done a fine job, not only in the field, but through their second battalions, in recruiting reinforcements. Those as mostly infantry units.
We are also endeavouring to recruit French-Canadian artillery and other technical units. In that connection, in order that there may be coordination, because artillery units cannot be used alone but in conjunction with divisional formations, we have sought to have a sufficient number in the artillery units who are bilingual, so that they can understand the directions which are given. And we have a school now which is opening up to give special instruction. I think it is in the interest of the country that we should do this for the French-Canadian boys who do not understand English, particularly those in the technical units, so that they will understand

the phrases and commands which are used, the articles which are referred to, and the orders which have to be communicated between their own and English units. We are doing that. We are endeavouring to form French-Canadian units and we are watching to see that our French-Canadians get fair representation, just so far as their qualifications permit.
I am sure that my hon. friend would not suggest on behalf of French-Canadians or anybody else in this country, at this time, when we need men who are equipped and trained and efficient that we should take men simply because of language or race unless they are efficient and have the necessary training. We are endeavouring to provide that training. My hon. friend will find that the French-Canadians stand up well in the officers' schools to which they go.
I do not think I can say any more, except to assure my friend that this subject is very much in my heart and in the hearts of the officers at headquarters. I know that he has not the same confidence in or the same warm feelings towards some of the officers at headquarters that I have, but I assure him, nevertheless, that the matter he speaks of is not being lost sight of either here or overseas, as he would know if he could see the exchange of cables which has taken place with regard to various French-Canadian appointments.

If I may ask one more
question, will it be possible for charitable organizations to get for the people in need in the poorer districts some of the used clothing from the Department of National Defence as was done before?

I cannot make any general statement on that. I received a very special application last night, an application on behalf of sufferers in the recent forest fires in Quebec province, and I did authorize the use of some unused and some discarded clothing for that purpose, to the extent of helping something like six hundred persons. But answering my hon. friend's question, each case will have to depend on its own merits.

I was not here yesterday
or on the last two occasions when the minister's estimates were before the committee and I wish to have about ten minutes this morning to offer to the government some constructive suggestions.
As to the point raised about home defence, there is no such thing as home defence in this country. The defence of this country, as I have pointed out before, is not going to be decided at Halifax or Vancouver or Saint

Supply-National Defence
John or Montreal. It is going to be decided in the primary theatre of war, in Britain and on the Mediterranean and on the Atlantic.
Canada up to the present has not in my opinion measured up to its responsibility as the senior dominion of this empire in the matter of home defence, as I interpret it. Home defence is not as important in Canada as in Great Britain, where the people are within range of enemy guns and are in danger of bombs falling on them every night.
On the question raised by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Cockeram) and replied to by the minister, there are certain amenities in British public life that I do' not find in Canada, and I believe that public questions should be discussed on certain principles as they are in England, where men are free to express divergent views. In the riding I represent I have held no public or other meetings and have discussed no politics whatsoever, only once a year to reelect officers. In my riding men and women's associations do nothing but war work.
At different times I have represented four or five ridings in the city of Toronto. I have been transferred around wherever there was a fight. But undoubtedly this is a different war from the last one, as the minister has said. In the old days a war might last only a matter of days. Now wars last for years and this one may last ten years in view of its widespread nature; it may break out again elsewhere. The war is different, too, because of the greater mechanization of the armed forces, the vast numbers of people involved and increased population. The hon. member for York South comes from the Toronto district. He is a soldier and belongs to a regiment I have not seen much of, but which the late Sir John Eaton and the late Colonel Boyd Magee many years ago came down with me to Ottawa to raise in the great war. Another was the 75th battalion. I was interested in a sort of city's own battalion.
I believe that a member of parliament should offer constructive criticism of the government, not of individuals in particular departments. The question that has arisen between the hon. member for York South and the Minister of National Defence arose in the British house in the days of Peel, Palmerston and the Crimean war, and this one. But in this war the principle was laid down both by Mr. Chamberlain when war broke out and by Mr. Churchill that a member of parliament can enter the British house wearing his uniform. It is the right and privilege of a soldier member of parliament to exercise the principles laid down by Burke in his address to the electors of Bristol, outlining the functions and duties of a member
of parliament, and stating that the exercise of his rights must not be interfered with. That relates to peace only, though. In war there must be of necessity some difference.
As I have said, in my constituency I have held no meetings since the war started except executive meetings for the election of officers once or twice a year. The hon. member for York South was within his privileges, as I see it, in making any criticism he saw fit to make in war time of the work of the department if he did it within the house. The minister in his reply, in effect, laid down the general principle followed now in the British house I believe. I notice that in the British, house in a week some forty-six questions were asked on the orders of the day on war and. defence, and they can ask supplementary questions there. We can here too according to-the evidence in 1929-30 by the committee which revised the rules. We are bound in the end by the British rules.
Turning to other matters I am glad that the minister has reduced soldiers' fares one-third; he did good work in that, I know. I hope that all charges for soldiers' fares will be eliminated next year. The hitch-hiking order should be rescinded, and I would like to see it done. The minister last year wrote a letter to me and to three or four other members of parliament about hitch-hiking and suggested that we had better appeal to the motor league. We did make an appeal, and I think the minister himself made a very strong appeal to motorists. That order ought to be rescinded, if I may respectfully suggest it. In England almost every car has a little sticker on the windshield, I am told, saying "Soldiers invited. Free rides." I was on the outskirts of Toronto at York Mills not long ago and one Sunday night I saw fifteen soldiers for Camp Borden trying to get a car ride, but everybody passed them by. On the 24th of May on my way to the Argonaut club secondary schools regatta, I passed two young soldiers in front of the exhibition grounds, and I saw the two still standing there on my way back an hour afterwards. I gave them a lift. The groom sat in the front seat. They belonged to the Irish regiment. I asked him where he came from, and he told me from such and such a street. "I am going to be married," he said, "at seven o'clock to-night by the chaplain." He said the soldier in the other seat is the best man; said he was a Scotsman and lived on Roncesvalles avenue,, which is in the riding of the hon. member for Parkdale, but he did not know him. I asked, him what school he went to. He said he was just out of Parkdale collegiate. I said I went there myself once. I asked the groom-to-be on what street he lived. He said that
Supply-National Defence

he lived on Pape avenue. I said, "Who is your member of parliament?" He said, "Tommy Church." He said to me, "Do you know him?" I said, "I never heard of him." Well, I took them to within a block or so of the place of the wedding. They asked me if it was right to go to the bride's home before the hour named with the best man. I said, no; sihe might change her mind. They askedi me to the wedding, but I did not go. But the point I wish to raise is the principle involved in this regulation.. I saw a thousand cars pass that baseball park in two hours on their way out to Sumnyside, on the road which, while I was chairman of the harbour commit sion, my board was responsible for constructing along twelve miles of waterfront. Those motorists are supposed not to help soldiers on. their way. They might do so, but did not.
I think that that hitch-hiking order has somewhat hurt recruiting, and I appeal to the minister to rescind it. I do not wish to offer the government anything but constructive suggestions, but criticism is a tonic and stirs governments to action, so long as it is founded on fact and is not actuated mainly by party bias or a desire to embarrass. The responsibility under our constitutional practice is on the government and minister. It is a heavy task at such a time as this. In my opinion the order is illegal, yet young fellows from Toronto who have enlisted in the service of their country are fined $5, which they can ill afford out of a week's pay. At Camp Borden you have a most able, popular and excellent officer. I am sorry to have to mention his camp in connection with this matter, because I do not wish a thing like hitch-hiking to interfere with a lifelong friendship for him. But I insist that the order is illegal, and I may mention that the provincial minister of highways, Hon. Mr. McQuesten, wrote to me that the Ontario government had never prosecuted a man under that order, and magistrates I have consulted tell me that they have never had a case like that before them. Why should a man getting only $1.30 a day be subjected to treatment of that kind? I appeal to the minister to reconsider this matter. He did good work in connection with the appeal for free fares; he approached the railways immediately and obtained some results. But the time has come when we should provide these men with free transportation, particularly when one remembers that 700,000 free civilian passes are issued every year.
Another matter should be mentioned at this time. The other day I travelled on the train with the chancellor of the university of Toronto on our way to the unveiling of the Macdonald memorial tablet. I do not often see the

chancellor, who is an old friend of mine, but I had occasion to observe some things which he did not seem to notice. At the rear of the morning train every morning recently, going to Kingston was one car which, when we stopped at Trenton, was soon filled by men of the air force. Indeed last Monday it was so packed with air force men and so overcrowded, there was no room for other soldiers who joined the same car at stations further on. I do not know why this overcrowding is necessary on the Canadian National Railways. Quite a number of cars used on Canadian National trains consist of old-fashioned carriages built at least thirty years ago. It is a shame that troops should be transported in that way all over Canada. They should have first-class accommodation. The minister wrote me and got some reform recently.
Then as to meals on the trains. The minister conferred with the management of both railways about a matter I raised as to the heavy cost of meals on trains, and secured some reduction in the cost of meals for soldiers. I am glad to see that, but in my opinion a corporation such as the Canadian National Railways which has spent vast sums on branch lines and entertainments, and which has received hundreds of millions of dollars from the public, should give further relief to the troops as to meals and trains and accommodation.
I believe the minister is making some inquiries about the records system. How does it come about that, in connection with the victory loan, announcements can be made every day in the newsapers of how many subscriptions by municipalities have been received, the amounts of individual subscription, and so on, when it is so difficult to get information about recruiting by municipalities? I know it is hard to do. I believe that there is need for a change in the records office system to the unit system. Last July the civic board of control allowed to General Alexander clerical civic help-three clerks to do this for Toronto for the army. I asked the Royal Canadian Air Force to do it for the manning pool. In June Deputy Minister Duncan said he could not do it, but in July again he wrote he would do it. Why cannot the records be segregated so as to show the figures with relation to every district, every municipality? These facts will have to be available when the war is over, if only to enable the authorities to deal with matters of old age pensions, relief, hospitalization and employment. I hope that something will be done in this connection, although I admit it will be a heavy task.

Supply-National Defence
Another matter which requires attention is the utilization of public property. I obtained a return with regard to what has been done by the various Canadian universities in Canada to supply the government with facilities. I will name just one university, the great university of Toronto, which did so much in the great war in arts and medicine and science and the noble contribution of graduates and splendid undergraduates, men who never came back. In that war the university of Toronto put all its buildings and other properties at the disposal of the Royal Flying Corps and army. The city did much the same; they turned over to the department, free of charge, all the exhibition grounds and splendid buildings which have a commercial value of $22,000,000. The school board lent free of charge all its buildings and other properties. I am not criticizing our great university in respect to the present war; far from it. They gave all that was asked, no doubt, but I notice that the government has rented various stores and properties near my own office and on our main streets. A building which is not fit for recruiting has been rented on Albert street. But little seems to have been done by institutions which enjoy exemption from taxation. The university of Toronto, the return shows, has contributed only a basement in the engineering building, and accommodation for a rifle range has been provided in a room at Hart house and a small house at 184 College street. But why should the government have to pay for practically all the accommodation it requires when there are exempt properties for education, schools and church property? The Ontario government has, in this respect, taken the lead among the provinces by making available to the department its properties at Guelph, St. Thomas,, and many other places, including new Ontario, and it is willing to give more. Yet the federal government has rented from the Quebec government a large property in Quebec for five years at a rental of $177,000, to be put to other uses no doubt later on.
A word with regard to the officers and the staff. The minister's predecessor, the lamented young gentleman who occupied that office at the outbreak of the war, wrote to members of parliament the second day after the war broke out asking us not to use any influence with the officials of the department to secure appointments for persons as commissioned officers and otherwise in the public service. I believe hon. members have respected that request. I know that I have, because I never got a man an appointment. I have been here since 1921, and I have yet to get any man an appointment any place in Ottawa; if I asked for it I know I would not get it, even to-day.
Reference was made last evening to Major General Harry Crerar. I have known his whole family for a great many years. I have not seen him since before this war began. It was a splendid appointment. He is a brother-in-law of the late Sir Adam Beck. His youngest brother, Malcolm, was killed in action when be was 19 years of age while serving with General Allenby. He had only been out of the Royal Military College about six months. The general and his other brother served in France in the great war. His mother, the late Mrs. P. D. Crerar and his sister, Lady Beck, were the finest patriotic workers in Canada. I am not here to defend him; he needs no defence. I believe he was recommended as the minister said by General McNaughton. However, there are one or two other brigadiers who I know Should not have been appointed. One of them, I was told by a fellow member here, claimed he had eight senators supporting him. Whether that is so or not I do not know, as the minister has said he is sure there is no political consideration given in such promotions although many others claim they can get no promotion.
One or two other things I wish to mention. The first is that of the soldiers' bonus. If by means of an act of parliament, or by rules of construction relating to it, we are to give a new bonus to certain officials in the Canadian National Railways, or to some of their officials who enlist for civilian and military work and still hold their positions and are not going to the war, something should be done in the matter of soldiers' free transportation. If anybody is to get a cost of living bonus the soldiers should get it; the men receiving the $1.30 a day should have some consideration as is the case of the civil service.
So far as home defence is concerned, I have already raised this question; I say that we have no home defence in municipalities, but local militia. They can have all the blackouts they like; they have some soldiers as home guard-they have already got it started as well as the air raid precautions I referred to here in 1938-39. My views on this matter were expressed as soon as the war broke out, and again in May, June and July of last year. I thought we should fallow the example of Finland, and train every man, woman and child to handle a rifle. I interviewed the present minister on the home guard matter. That is the proper course for a sparsely populated country like Canada. There is no use in letting the people think they are protected with black-outs, trying to persuade the people of Canada, in every municipality, that they have home defence when they have nothing of the kind, suggesting that we are
Supply-National Defence

armed for an emergency in all places, when in some towns and small places we have not so much as a pinwheel, a firecracker or a skyrocket for home defence. The hon. member for Temiscouata, when speaking the other day on the needs of his own constituency for defence remarked that you cannot blow your nose in this house without saying that it is for the war effort: everything is "for the war effort".
We are assured that the British government consents and agrees to everything which this government has done. That is the reply given to everything mentioned. I do not know whether they consented to the hon. member here blowing his nose and agreed that that too is part of the war effort. But everything, it is said, is consented to by the British government; they asked for it, and it is all right; and this we are expected to believe, without any document supporting it, because somebody says so.
In my opinion people should be told the truth and the grave danger we are in. So far as the municipalities are concerned, there is no such thing as home defence. I discussed last July the question of air raid precautions with the minister and the deputy minister as to adopting the Finland way. I did so three months before the matter was taken up by the provincial authorities in Ontario. I suggest that we should follow the example of Finland and have every man, woman and child taught to handle a rifle. Miniature ranges should be established all over Canada as the first step in local defence, and air raid precautions also are necessary.
We have an information department which is known here as the publicity bureau. That is the only bit of humour I have heard during the session apart from one or two other examples. A publicity bureau giving only propaganda information.
I was speaking a little while ago about the amenities of British public life. As we all know, pacifists like Morrison, Alexander, MacDonald and others one could mention were promoted to the cabinet. The First Lord of the Admiralty, Mr. Alexander, reduced the navy from 72 to 50 capital ships, would not build destroyers, and Britain was no longer a first class power. Mr. Morrison, head of the London County Council would not allow certain facilities or buildings to be used by the air force three years ago, and Mr. MacDonald a pacifist, who helped with the Irish bases, was league-minded. Our information bureau now has at its head a gentleman who was a pacifist and isolationist, who introduced into the house on March 31, 1939, a bill which I talked out, because it had for its purpose the declaration that when war

came we would be neutral and parliament would decide. I objected to our small militia votes.
Who is to blame for the absolutely defenceless position of the country when war broke out? The answer is that all parties were responsible, because, almost everyone in the house seemed to be saturated with the Geneva fad, the Geneva nonsense, with the result that we reduced our army, our air force and our navy to practically nothing- so much so that Hitler thought that some of the dominions would not come to the support of the motherland but would remain neutral.
As regards the question of theatres of war, it is my opinion that the primary theatre, Great Britain, should be looked after. Canada has only 80,000 troops in England. We should have a large army over there so that when Britain has achieved the mastery of the air they might help Britain take the offensive, with the aid of the fleet.
Coming to the question of cadet services, I may say that at one time I was the only member of parliament who stood up for this highly essential institution when every attempt was made to abolish it in the years from 1932 to 1937. In fact, it was abolished by the school board of Toronto. But if it had not been for the cadet services, away back in the time of the Northwest rebellion and the south African war as well as in the last great war and this present struggle, I do not know where the militia would have been in Toronto. The cadet services are a valuable auxiliary, and always the backbone of the militia.
As regards the medical services, the minister stated that 14,000 men had been discharged since the war started. In the pension committee I think the figure given was 1,800 in one month. The minister of pensions has done good work in pensions, as he did previously when at the head of the army, and I trust these men will be generously dealt with.
The only question I should like to discuss for a moment now in conclusion is one that was raised by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce). I have myself discussed it on four or five different occasions. I say now that we could have done better, even under a voluntary system, and could have had a volunteer army of 750,000, if recruiting had been encouraged, instead of on again, off again, on again. The present minister is not altogether to blame, because he took over the department when recruiting had fallen down and enthusiasm had been somewhat spent. The fact is that nothing w'as done to encourage young men who were eager to enlist at the right time and tried to get

Supply-National Defence
in. I remember seeing outside the armouries in Toronto at 9 a.m., men who stood there between the hours of six and nine in the morning on January 6, 1940, when it was eight below zero, a line-up of men who quite obviously were anxious to get into the army; but these men were not even allowed to go into the armouries so as to get out of the cold. Here are the newspaper pictures of it. There were young fellows from Mimico and Aurora and other districts who were wearing sweaters at the time, and many of these young fellows had to get a meal at the Scott institute. There has been a considerable improvement, but I suggest that if the minister cannot get recruits he should adopt some other method. He should study the situation critically between now and the time parliament reassembles and be prepared to make a report that will satisfy the people as to whether it is necessary to take other methods. We compel our citizens to be educated in order to be able to take their places in civil life, and I do not see why one of the first essentials of education for responsible citizenship should not be training to fit men to defend their homes and their country. If we compel every worker to insure himself against the chances of unemployment in industrial life, while working with the vast mechanization of to-day, and the discoveries in arts and science and other matters, why not also equally to insure oneself and one's fellows against this present German disaster, which means not only loss of wages but of the very life worth living for free men. The only European countries which did not have compulsory service were little Luxemburg and Vatican city.
Australia and New Zealand have had compulsory training and service for home defence for many years-true for home defence mostly, as they are so close to Japan.
Conscription is the only system that is just to all; the pity of it is that in the last war it was mixed up with politics and never had a chance. If we had run the voluntary system properly it would not be necessary. As I said in 1937 and 1938, the most exposed provinces are the maritimes, Quebec and British Columbia. Are we going to wait until the enemy appears on our own soil, as it did in the small countries of Europe, with its vast mechanization, and brutality and savagery, before we get a proper army, navy and air force and raise a million men?
With regard to recruiting, we could have had 750,000 men under the voluntary system if we had gone about it properly. Compulsory national service is the most democratic system that could possibly be devised. Under such a system none can complain. All are
treated alike; all are required to render the same sort of service, to submit to the same system of discipline. Nothing increases so much the spirit of loyalty and patriotism as service. To make every citizen feel that he, individually, is part of the defensive force of the country would make him justly proud; the physical and mental training and discipline and practical instruction which is part of the education of a soldier to-day, would make him a more valuable citizen in every way, and the time spent in his military service would be returned to him many-fold in increase of efficiency and ability for sustained and disciplined effort in all his subsequent career.
National service is fair in principle, avoids discrimination and the practice of substitution or securing an exemption by payment of a stipulated amount. It makes a better man, a self-respecting man-in all, a better citizen. We can only become really strong and invincible when every man in the broad expanse of our land. can be taught cheerfully to recognize his obligation of service and to take pride and satisfaction in the knowledge that he is a qualified defender of our common liberties and one of the guardians of this glorious land.
By the New York State constitution, all ablebodied male citizens between the ages of eighteen and forty-five, who are residents, of the state, constitute the militia. There is' no more danger of our nation becoming militaristic through preparedness than there was that the students of colleges would become ruffians or prize-fighters when the colleges made attendance in the gymnasium compulsory. There is more danger of militarism from unpreparedness than from the maintenance of a sufficient army and navy. Can anyone doubt that any great defeat suffered by this country in war would change this country to a militaristic nation, because the man of the sword would become the national hero, since through him our national rights could most potently be restored?
The late Mr. Hamilton Merritt in his book on national service, is responsible for the last fifteen lines which I have quoted with reference to the state of New York.
I have just a few more words to say. I have received a letter from a lady who has a son in Singapore. He has been with the navy and has been anxious to come home on leave. He has six months' leave, but the foreign exchange control board will not give him any Canadian funds to come home, and his father and mother are ill. I do not like to be sending the minister letters all the time. If all members send him letters it would mean. 245 multiplied. Also a traveller on the train from Montreal met a boy the other day whose mother had died. He had no funds with which to get home; he had had a hard
Supply-National Defence

time getting enough together to get him to Toronto and it will cost him three weeks [DOT] pay. I hope the minister will be able to arrange for a fund of some kind to take care of cases like this. I apologize for detaining the committee, but I represent a military district and I get a great many complaints. They do not all belong to my riding, but for some reason or other they write to me. I should be glad if a lot of them would write to somebody else, because I do not want to take up the time of the house and of our overworked officials.
We do not know where we are going to be until we come back here. Everything is as usual in Canada and every member of parliament should see that it is not as usual. You cannot go into any amusement place without seeing it. I had a complaint this morning from a man whose son was killed in the present war off England. He served with the 1st battalion in the last war and he complains that people are asking him to enlist. The boy's mother has received some kind of cross from the government which she appreciates very much, but the father has been stopped, even by soldiers, and asked to enlist. I think such men should be given some sort of button to wear.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to commend the very encouraging statement made this morning by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and express the hope that it will have a splendid effect upon the morale of our people. I also hope that the spirit as well as the words of that statement will be carried out. If the facts were given to this house, as they are in the British House of Commons, I am sure that we would all agree with what the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mrs. Casselman) is reported to have said a few days ago. I quote:
I see no value in criticizing until fully informed upon a subject, and then being prepared to offer suggestions for improvement.
May I digress for a moment to congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton East upon her recent success at the polls and to voice the opinion that by her grace and culture she will prove a valuable addition to this house. My only regret is that the whip did not see fit to place her opposite these benches.
Although the Minister for National Defence (Mr. Ralston) placed the blame for the lack of essential equipment for the troops in Canada upon the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe)-
I must interrupt my hon. friend. I have placed no such blame. My hon. friend is used to making that sort of insinuation and I ask him to withdraw that statement. He will not find it anywhere.
That was my interpretation.
My hon. friend has no right to say that. I ask him to point to a single sentence upon which that interpretation could be placed. My hon. friend is too prone to do this sort of thing.
May I just finish my statement?

I am interrupting to object to my hon. friend stating that I placed the blame for lack of equipment upon the Minister of Munitions and Supply. That is absolutely untrue. There is nothing in the records to justify that or from which my hon. friend could make an interpretation of the kind.
I shall leave that to members of the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
A point of order has
been raised in connection with statements made by the hon. member for Parkdale reflecting upon something that has been done by the Minister of National Defence. The Minister of National Defence raises a point of order and has made a statement with respect to his own declarations and with respect to his own actions. Under the rules of the house an hon. member must accept a statement made by another hon. member with respect to what he said or did not say. Therefore, I request the hon. member for Parkdale to withdraw the remark from which such inference could be drawn.

I abide by your ruling, and I am glad to withdraw the conclusion which I thought I was justified in arriving at from the remarks made last evening by the Minister of National Defence.
The Minister of National Defence will then have to assume responsibility himself for the deplorable situation disclosed by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Cockeram). As he pointed out, there has been widespread dissatisfaction with the functioning of the defence department, which I believe is partly due to the confusion engendered by the constant changing of plans for training. That is not only my own view; it is held by others. I should like to quote as evidence an article written by Mr. Williamson, a veteran of the last war and now secretary of the Canadian

Supply-National Defence
corps. This is entitled "We can't run two armies" and was published in Saturday Night of Ma}' 10. It reads:
There should be only one army and it should be an extremely active army. Canada is not defensible with any force that we could raise. If Britain falls, we fall. An army for home defence may contribute to that fall. It will sap the strength of the overseas army. It will take men, money and equipment. It will add complication to an already muddled situation. The thirty-day and four-month schemes were bad enough in all conscience, but to immobilize thousands of our young men for duration is madness. It would unnecessarily impede our industrial output; it would be unfair to the voluntary army overseas, and it would add nothing to the safety of the country.
The utter failure of the reserve army, as a source of reinforcements, must now be plain to all. It is no longer to be considered as a reserve. It is to be moved to the sea-boards as an army for Canada's defence, a duty it could never perform. Its failure is so abject that already it is proposed that units of the third and fourth divisions are to be broken up for reinforcements. This did not happen in the great war until four divisions had gone through the hells of Passchendaele and the Somme. With the announcement of the latest scheme, it is admitted that it never was in fact' an effective reserve. The minister now says that the organized units were, in great part, composed of men unfit for service or of those who, for personal reasons, could not go overseas. It may be nothing more than stupidity that has brought us to this pass, but the government is not keeping faith with the men who have volunteered. It has gambled, and to-day is gambling with the existence of the empire and of Canada at stake. There must be one army and one type of enlistment from this point on. Battalions of veterans and lower category men can undertake such duties as are necessary in Canada.
I received a clipping the other day from the Winnipeg Tribune of May 28 containing a letter in favour of conscription. I shall not read the letter, but I should like to refer to the editor's footnote which is as follows:
Recruiting figures show that the number of active service force volunteers, per thousand of population, is higher for French-Canadians than for English-speaking Canadians.
No one would be more pleased than I if that were true, but so far as I am aware no reply has been given by the minister to the questions which have been asked in connection with recruiting in the various provinces, unless it was his speech of May 12 last, when he said:
The thirty-day plan for compulsory training was accepted by every province including Quebec. The four-month compulsory training plan was accepted by every province. I may say that young men in the province of Quebec have come to the camps in larger surplus numbers perhaps than in any other province.
I submit that this statement does not justify the interpretation placed upon these words by the editor, and I would ask the minister to
clarify the situation by giving the figures previously asked for, as well as the figures to date, of active service force volunteers per thousand of population, of French-Canadians and of English-speaking Canadians respectively, so that there may be no cause for misunderstanding. I think it would be very helpful if the minister also would give a break-down of the recruiting figures for the various military districts in Canada up to date, showing first the number enlisted for active service overseas, and second those enlisted for home defence. In this connection I should like to ask the minister if any of the men previously discharged from the army for the reason that they were not regarded as likely to become efficient soldiers are being reenlisted. I am informed that this is so.
Heretofore we have been lulled into a sense of false security by the statements made in this house that more men were not needed. Can anyone doubt to-day that men were urgently needed, when one recalls with chagrin what happened in Libya, in Greece and in Crete, where British armies suffered a severe defeat because of lack of man power? Still more men will be needed if we are to play our part as lojrally as have the other dominions of this empire.
The Minister of National Defence is modestly asking for 32,000 men. Has he any expectation that this will meet even our immediate needs? I venture to say that if Canada is to play its part proportionately to the other dominions we will need to raise at least 300,000 men, Instead of four divisions we should now have twice that number. A Canadian Press dispatch from Hamilton, New York, dated June 9, containing a report of the speech made by the minister to the graduates of Colgate university, at which time he received an honorary degree-on which I wish to congratulate him-contains this statement:
When war began, we had 10,500 men on active service in the three fighting services, and to-day in those services we have a quarter of a million men enlisted to serve wherever duty may require them, together with a reserve army of 175,000, subject to call for the defence of Canada.
This makes a total of 425,000. Since this figure very greatly exceeds the figures given to this house so far by the minister in regard to those on active service who have enlisted for duty anywhere, will the minister say whether or not he was correctly reported?

I can say now to my hon. friend that I am correctly reported. That statement has been made frequently.
Supply-National Defence

I understand that we have had a third Canadian division at Debert for about a year. I should like to ask the minister if they have received sufficient training to be ready for active service, to face the enemy on equal terms. If not, is there any reason why they should not receive that training in Canada? If these troops can be trained in Canada, and I see no reason why they should not be trained here, then to me it would seem almost a criminal imposition upon the hospitality of an overcrowded, harassed England, to ask them to provide food and space to enable these troops to complete their training after they arrive in that country.
As a veteran of the last war I feel it incumbent upon me to express disagreement with the attitude of the minister towards members of the reserve army who are also members of this house, in respect to their right of criticism either inside or outside this house, in connection with the preparedness of the armed forces. I do not propose to enter into a discussion of military law, upon which the king's regulations and orders are based, but I should like to quote from a speech made by Mr. Churchill in the British House of Commons on November 21, 1940:
I entirely agree with what has been said about the desirability of members of parliament serving not only in the military services but in all other forms of warfare and discharging their parliamentary duties at the same time or in alternation. No doubt difficulties arise, but I think they are well covered, and that the good sense of the house and of hon. members will enable these dual and occasionally conflicting functions to be discharged.
During the last war, as well as this war, there have been notable instances of such criticism in the British House of Commons. For instance, Admiral Keyes spoke in criticism of the Norwegian fiasco, and during the last war Admiral Beresford also criticized the government. If this can go on in England under the stress of war surely it would have been better if the Minister of National Defence had not insisted on too legal an interpretation of the words rather than the spirit of the king's regulations and order.
Mr. Churchill was talking about speeches in parliament. I have raised no objection to speeches in parliament.
I think I am right in assuming that the minister did object formally in the house.
Well, if my hon. friend has another assumption or impression or interpretation I am saying that I did not.

Of course I am bound to accept the minister's statement. I would

suggest to him that criticism is often the truest form of loyalty. Prime Minister Churchill evidently thought so, for in his statement in the British house a few days ago he said:
No one, however ministerially minded, could possibly complain of the tone, temper and matter of this debate. The kind of criticism we have had to-day-some of it very searching -is the kind that the government not only accepts but welcomes.
May I express the hope that the ministerial benches will profit by this statement by Mr. Churchill.
I adopt that statement of Mr. Churchill's in November.
I am very glad to hear the minister make that statement.
That is exactly what I was suggesting, that there would be conflicts from time to time and that I thought they could be reconciled; and that is what Mr. Churchill has said.

I had not intended during this session to reply to the minister's totally unjustifiable attack upon me on May 12 lost, but since the subject has been again opened I feel called upon to make some comment.
It was a little over a month ago that I recommended selective compulsory enlistment as the only fair and efficient way to meet the complex needs of Canada. As I stated then, I now repeat, I spoke then and now speak only for myself. The minister characterized my remarks as a blow at our national unity and, whether I intended it or not, an attempt to undermine it. I entirely dissent from that view. In my belief there is nothing that would better promote national unity than the idea that every citizen in Canada, irrespective of his racial origin, is playing an equal part in this great struggle.
The other day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) stated that equality of sacrifice, according to ability to pay, has been the basis for taxation. I ask that equality of sacrifice, according to the ability to serve, should also be the basis for enlistment. I believe that one large section of our population, the FrenclnCanadians of Quebec, are as much concerned about the preservation of their freedom and the survival of the British empire as are any other sections in Canada. To suggest otherwise is an insult to their loyalty.
I should now like to quote from a French-Canadian newspaper to show the changed attitude in that province in respect of Canada's participation in war outside of Canada. I

Supply-National Defence
hold in my hand an editorial from Le Soleil of Quebec, June 4, 1941, and, I quote in part, as follows:
It could not be otherwise, because we are the most genuine and the truest Canadians. We have said that among us, as in all the other provinces, there will always be a sufficient number of volunteers to defend our country- even if to defend Canada it is necessary to meet the enemy on another ground to prevent them from coming here. No intelligent and bona fide Canadian doubts this. On the other hand, everything shows that Canada is menaced. The theatre of war is enlarging. Who would refuse to admit that it is better to prevent Canada from becoming a battle field? That it is better to spare our women and children the unfortunate lot of the women and children of Europe? That it is better to meet the enemy where they are and halt them in their march toward America?
I am afraid, however, that the question has been approached rather from the point of view of political expediency than in any other way. I may say quite frankly that at the present time I am not concerned about the fortunes of any political party, but I am concerned about the survival of Canada as an integral part of the British empire. If we lost this war HitleT would very soon get rid of all political parties, as well as our democratic way of life. Nearly a year ago the United States, although not at war, called up 1,000,000 men for compulsory selective draft. I believe the word "draft" is a better word than the one which I did not use in my former speech, but which was used by the minister himself- "conscription".
Surely after nearly twenty-two months of war, and with the disasters which have happened in Europe staring us in the face, we should now be eager to throw aside all political considerations, and to face stern realities. We should be ready to adopt the speediest and fairest means of securing man power to meet immediate and future needs, both in the field and in the factories.
That means conscription of labour, as well, does it? That is the way I would understand it. I am asking my hon. friend if that is what he does mean.

I believe a system of selective draft for all, whether in the army or otherwise, is the better way. It was accepted in the United States without protest, and it did not cause disunity, because the president was wise enough to call into his cabinet two outstanding Republicans, Mr. Stimson and Mr. Knox.
A few evenings ago we listened to an almost frantic appeal from Lord Beaverbrook for more tanks, more ships, more aeroplanes and more men. He said that life was in the balance, and made an urgent appeal for more help from Canada. The Hon. Ronald Cross,
on his way to Australia, expressed himself in similar terms. These men I submit are in a most advantageous position to know what the real needs of the present situation are overseas.
When in his speech on May 12 the minister referred to me as one who spoke glibly and without thought, he made an incorrect statement. When I advocated a change in the system I spoke only after the most mature consideration. I would point out to him that it is the realist who is serving Canada and the empire best at this time. I would also give him the same reply I gave to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) on June 5, 1940, when I spoke in the house regarding Canada's ability to make tanks. The Minister of Munitions and Supply said as reported at page 309 of Hansard 1940-and I took it that he was referring to me, and to something I had said on May 28, 1940-
So when a man stands up and makes reckless statements about two firms in Hamilton that can build tanks-
And so on. I replied as follows:
I wish to tell the minister that I am not in the habit of making reckless statements.
And I say to the minister of defence that I am not in the habit of speaking glibly in the house.
My whole training and habit of life have been to observe scientific accuracy, and I resent the minister's accusation.
The Minister of Labour in England, Hon. Ernest Bevin, speaking on June 6 in the British House of Commons, said that the next three months will be the most vital in our history-a forecast which may be only too accurate.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee took recess I was about to speak of a matter to which I referred in a resolution which I put on the order paper on June 3 last, and which reads as follows:
Whereas criticism has been made regarding the lack of any recognized comprehensive training plan to which training can be adjusted, as distinguished from our military plans of operation,
Therefore be it resolved that, in the opinion of this house, a planning committee should be set up to devise a training plan in keeping with the tremendous changes that have taken place in military science since the beginning of this war.
I would not venture personally to suggest a training plan but I am going to give a brief synopsis of a training plan proposed by a
Supply-National Defence

competent artillery officer who served in the last war and who has been connected with artiltery organizations ever since. He says:
Officers of vision and imagination should be chosen to constitute a military planning committee for the purpose of devising a master training plan.
Might Canada not be used as the training ground for the main hitting force (or shock troops) which will be used for victory? The Canadian corps was used as shock troops in many historic battles in the last war. These "shock troops" are highly specialized men whose job it is to break the resistance of the enemy and pave the way for the movement of the larger formations.
The "shock troops" are armoured divisions working in close cooperation with aircraft specially trained for this work. The larger formations already organized to resist invasion in the British isles, added to their normal dense population and the difficulty created by German air raiders, will add enormously to the task of training specialized "shock troops" needed in modern offensive.
The same ideal conditions found in Canada, which have enabled us to make a great success of the commonwealth air training plan, exist for the specialized training of armoured divisions.
It is believed by competent military authorities that ultimate victory depends upon the organization of a larger number of extremely mobile armoured fighting units, manned by a relatively small number of highly trained men. It is almost impossible to give adequate training for this purpose in Great Britain. No country in the world is more admirably suited for this purpose than is Canada. If this is to be our role, then Canada should specialize in the training and coordination of land and air forces suitable for attack.
Referring further to the training plan he says:
It may be necessary to create a distinct air army for the armoured fighting forces.
Germany did not delay her training until she had all necessary equipment, guns, et cetera. She used improvised equipment.
One thing that will probably attract recruits more than anything else is the knowledge that their time will not be wasted and that from the very day they enlisted their abilities will be directed into useful channels. In the opinion of many competent officers, nothing is deterring recruiting more at the present time than the fact that our young men know how ineffective the training of our land forces really is. Such methods, i.e., the use of improvised equipment, were used by Germany for years and it would be futile to deny the effectiveness of the methods they adopted for training for land forces. The urgency for such a national training plan has been stressed on many occasions by representative military groups dnd the urgency becomes more apparent every day as we sit by and read of continued German victories.
I think the best answer I can give to the minister's charge that I was attempting to drive a wedge of disunity into Canada's war

effort and that my suggestion was ill-timed and unnecessary will be to quote from a letter of Major-General Elmsley, D.S.O., C.M.G., appearing in the Globe and Mail about a week ago. General Elmsley was chief of staff at military headquarters here and is one of Canada's most distinguished soldiers. He spent thirty-three years as a professional soldier, of which seven were spent in war, which should surely equip him to speak with knowledge and authority; and I think his opinion should command the respect of all. The letter to which I refer will be found in the Globe and Mail of June 7. I quote it only in part. General Elmsley says:
Conscription honestly administered without political interference ensures equality of sacrifice, and equality of sacrifice in a democracy ensures unity. What, then, is this question of disunity that is referred to so often by politicians but never openly discussed in actual words?
We of Ontario and other provinces feel that Quebec has been represented by the existing government as irrevocably opposed, en masse, to conscription. This I cannot believe, for two reasons.
1.	As a Roman Catholic I am of the same religion as the majority of the people of Quebec, and our church maintains that we should take up arms in support of our government in a just war, and there is admittedly no question about the justness of this war. No Roman Catholic either of Quebec or of any other province can therefore refuse his armed support to his government on religious grounds.
2.	As a soldier by profession of thirty-three years' service and of this seven years spent in war, may I state that I have served under French-Canadians as my superior officers, with French-Canadians as my equals and under me, and they have proved repeatedly in peace and in war that they are a gallant and honourable people. . . .

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member should say that to Doctor Shields.

He will probably be able to
read that.
Colonel Ralston has stated publicly that there is no need for conscription. Others have said with equal emphasis that we have come to the end of our resources of man power on a voluntary basis of enlistment. Only the results of the present appeal for an additional 32,000 men on a voluntary basis will give an indication of the correctness of these claims. It is certain, however, that heavy fighting and heavy casualties are bound to occur in the near future, and the question will arise shortly whether our war effort overseas is to be restricted by the use of volunteers only, or whether the whole of our man power is to be utilized under conscription.
History has shown that conscription enforced unexpectedly in a panic or emergency-and an emergency may arise in a matter of weeks or months-is a criminal disservice, as it creates bitterness and distrust among fighting men who have enlisted on a voluntary basis and those who have enlisted on a compulsory basis, and

Supply-National Defence
furthermore disrupts our war industries by introducing grave disputes between the employers of labour and the requirements of our fighting services.
Conscription should be discussed now, and if deemed advisable adopted forthwith.
He concludes by saying:
We cannot serve two masters in this war, that is, the cause of our king, Great Britain and our sister dominions on the one hand, and our local political interests on the other. These interests are obviously not identical and will, therefore, come into conflict to the detriment of our fighting activities.
In view of what the minister said this morning, I should like to call attention to the rebuke which he administered to the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough when he spoke in this house on March 11, as reported in Hansard at page 1416. I wonder what has caused the minister to change his views since 1917, when he was serving in France in his majesty's forces, as to the freedom allowed officers. The minister did not hesitate at that time to take part in a political campaign in Canada, although he was not a candidate. According to the Halifax Chronicle of December 14, 1917, he sent the following cable to A. K. Maclean, the candidate of union government for Halifax:
France, Dec. 12, 1917.
I strongly favour the immediate operation of the Military Service Act, and hope Nova Scotia will heavily support candidates pledged to that policy.
Ralston.
I should like to ask the minister if he considers the situation to-day less critical than it was in December, 1917. At that time we had the support of Russia, the powerful fleets of Japan, and Italy, unbeaten France with its superb army, and the help as an ally of the great United States of America, in addition to receiving supplies from many neutral countries all of which are now under the heel of Hitler; while to-day, Great Britain fights alone.

Let me at once refer to two or three points which my hon. friend has brought up.
Regarding the training of the army, with all due deference to him I prefer to accept the advice of the officers who know conditions overseas, who have been overseas, who have been in close touch, not only with General McNaughton, but with the staff overseas of the war office, from the chief of the Imperial General Staff down, and who therefore have some idea of the requirements of training in this country.
Let me say further that while I respect General Elmsley's views as a military man,
the opinion he expresses with regard to conscription is expressed not in his capacity as a military man but in his capacity as a citizen of this country, just the same as anybody else. So I do not think that all the build-up which my hon. friend has given to General Elmsley in connection with his military record has anything much to do with the soundness or otherwise of his expression of opinion as a civilian upon this particular question.
It shows his experience.

It shows his experience as a military man, but my hon. friend is quoting his opinion on a matter quite apart from his military experience.
Let me now come to the matter dealt with by my hon. friend in the last three minutes of his speech, in which he observed that in 1917 I favoured the national service act of that time. My hon. friend asks, what is the difference between now and then? Let me tell him. At that time we were in the third year of the great war; in fact it had been going on for nearly three years and a quarter. So far, the present war has lasted for about twenty months, and in all three services we have had probably seven hundred casualties. Up to December of 1917 Canadian casualties were numbered in the tens of thousands. Already the fifth division had had to be broken up in order to furnish reinforcements. When that telegram was sent, I, as an officer of a battalion, had had the experience of receiving men from dismantled battalions from all over Canada-units which had had to be broken up in order to provide reinforcements to replace casualties. At that time the battle of Passachendaele had just been fought and the Canadian corps had been decimated. The casualties in my own battalion in the two days we were engaged numbered between four and five hundred, of which 138 were killed. That was the condition in December, 1917. What is the condition in Canada to-day? It is that we have enlisted less men at this time than we had at the corresponding stage of the last war, that we have had comparatively few casualties, that the army has not been in action, although it is holding a strategic position in England at the suggestion and request of the British government. I say to my hon. friend that, at that time, recruiting campaign after recruiting campaign had been put on in Canada, from one end to the other. I myself in the spring of 1916, a year a half after war was declared, was engaged in an intensive volunteer recruiting campaign, and after that time, battalion after battalion after battalion was raised in this country under the volunteer system.
