So that the condition then and the condition now cannot be compared. We are at this time, as I pointed out the other day, engaged in the first intensive campaign for recruits since this war began-the very first. And I ask my hon. friend again in all seriousness as a citizen of Canada: Why raise this question of conscription at this time? He knows that in 1917 it split Canada from top to bottom.
We had at that time no such united position as we have in Canada to-day. As I said the other day, in October, one m'onth after war was declared, the province of Quebec had an election on the issue as to whether they would participate in this war. What did they do? They voted overwhelmingly to stand with Canada in the war-to stand with Canada, who was standing by the side of Britain. That was followed by compulsory training, known as the thirty-day training scheme. That plan was advised by the chief of the general staff, and put into effect. I venture to say it did a great deal to bring the young men of Canada-not simply the young men of Quebec- to a realization that there was a national duty to perform. Eighty thousand men were trained at that time. That was followed by the four months training plan, whereby the men took not only basic training, but advanced training as well. That was put into effect. Both those plans were accepted all over the Dominion of Canada, without exception anywhere. Then the plan was announced which stated that those who had their four months' training would be drafted-to use my hon. friend's expression-for service in Canada. That, too, was accepted all across Canada.
Having regard to that situation, and to the unity which undoubtedly prevails, I really feel my hon. friend is not doing a service to Canada at this time when he advocates conscription. Probably this afternoon the premier of Quebec will be doing what? He will be asking the young men of Quebec to volunteer to enlist in connection with this recruiting campaign. That is an example of unity. I ask my hon. friend why he wishes to introduce this discordant note at a time when we are engaged in raising recruits. The effect of it is-and my hon. friend must be able to see this-that it provides a young man who may doubt whether he needs to enlist with a reason for delaying to do so. It hinders the war effort, as I said the. other day; and it hinders the campaign which is going on across Canada at the present time.
It will be noticed that my hon. friend is not advocating anything of this kind in regard to money. I have no doubt that he is serving on some kind of committee. He is no doubt asking Canadians to subscribe their money to our war loan. But my hon. friend

suggests that we pass a law right now before we have really tried the volunteer system, fold our arms, and request these young men to come in.
Some suggestion has been made about compulsory service in other dominions. I made a mistake myself the other day, and I wish to correct it. In New Zealand there is provision for compulsory service but in the other dominions, Australia and south Africa there is no such law. Enlistments are voluntary.
I say to my hon. friend I had the feeling that at this time he might-and those who think as he does-help in every way possible in connection with this campaign to get men. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that this campaign will do a great deal in the Dominion of Canada to encourage future enlistment. I must agree with those who say that we have not put to the young men of Canada, perhaps as we should, the need for men. I agree that we did not take all the men that were offered. Why? Because-I can say this now, as I said it the other day-because conditions were such, in connection with shipping, that we could not send overseas the men we intended to. We were having to shift plans from time to time. There was a necessity for accommodation. There was a necessity for armament. It was considered that recruiting could be allowed to take its normal course according to our needs. We began recruiting again in February, I think it was. The number recruited did not come up to the quota, which meant that next month you had to add to that month the deficiency of the month before, and so on with the next month. That is one of the reasons for the call for recruits now in this first intensive recruiting campaign that has been put on.
But that was not the only reason by any means. Another was that establishments, particularly in connection with the technical units, were increased, and men who had been expected to be used for reinforcements were used instead to fill up those increased establishments.
Another reason was, and is, that we took the men out of the technical units from the fourth division to form the armoured division. We did not plan to build the fourth division up until some time later, but we decided in view of the situation to accelerate that, and we are now asking for something like 8,000 men for the fourth division.
Then there were discharges on medical grounds which were greater than we expected. When I found there was doubt as to the phj'sical capacity of some men, and I have in mind particularly certain units, to stand the strain, as I wanted to see that we sent

Supply-National Defence
over to Great Britain an army that could stand up with any of them, I insisted that there be a further medical examination. That examination was made, a large number of men were discharged, and that adds of course to the number we are requiring and asking for to-day.
We are making a special call for 32,000 recruits, and there will be the quotas from month to month to make up wastage. But I believe that if we educate the people of Canada now in connection with this recruiting campaign as to the need for men from this time on, and if we have them realize that there is a situation which demands their support, we shall get it and the impetus given by this campaign will assist us with the further quotas needed.
That is the position. My hon. friend and I differ in connection with it but I deprecate again my hon. friend bringing this question up before we have even really tried out the voluntary system in Canada.
With regard to the other matters to which my hon. friend has referred, I do not think there is very much point in my going over them in detail at this late stage of the session. He has dealt extensively with training. I have already received a letter and a memorandum from the author of the memorandum which my hon. friend read to the committee to-day, and I have had that memorandum examined, sentence by sentence, by the training officers of the department. I have had it examined, not in a spirit of defence or in a spirit of excuse, but to see what there was in it that was good and that we could make use of, to stack up the suggestions made therein against actual performance, against what is being done to-day, and to adopt any remedial measures when such seemed to be indicated. Certain suggestions I think in the light of the experience of the training officers, particularly the experience we have had overseas, would not prove to be sound. But in so far as the-memorandum makes constructive suggestions which can be used, I assure my hon. friend they will be used.
I do not propose to follow my hon. friend in connection with the other matters he mentioned. Let me just say this:	The man
who is speaking to you to-day has a fairly heavy task. I need all the help and all the support I can possibly get. I believe that in the interests of Canada at this time the thing to do is to drive on with this recruiting campaign and have young men realize that young men are needed and ask them to come in, and I propose to do that. I believe I would not be a good Canadian if I did not do that. That is my position, and I ask my
hon. friend and all others to put their shoulders to the wheel in connection with this campaign, and instead of suggesting alternative methods in the middle of the recruiting campaign, to endeavour to assist in every way possible to impress on young men that they are required and the attractions of service for Canada in her hour of need.
May I say just a word to the hon. member for Broadview. He brought up quite a few questions, and I am not going to deal with them in detail. I only say to him, as I have had to say to him before, that the suggestions which he has made will be considered. I have given a good deal of thought to some of the subjects to which he has referred, and he knows I have had a good deal of correspondence with him. I do want to say one word, and it is because the man is not here to answer for himself. The hon. member introduced-perhaps through inadvertence- but I would not want it to remain on the record as it is-the suggestion that General Crerar was selected on the suggestion of- I understood him to say-"a late senator". I do not know to whom he refers. I have no idea who he is talking about. All I want to say is that no suggestion of any kind or description came from any senator or any member of the House of Commons or, for that matter, anyone on this side of the water with regard to the selection of General Crerar. The selection was made, as I said last night, and I give my word to the house for this, solely on the recommendation of General McNaughton after I had a personal conversation with him and after he had considered the matter fully.
I am not going to take up the time of the committee any longer. I only say that I feel from the bottom of my heart that we are trying to do a job in the Department of National Defence. I have said time and time again, and I repeat, that we are not content or satisfied. I can only pledge to the house that I will give my best in order to see the job through.

As I listened to the concluding words of the Minister of National Defence with reference to those who would at this time raise one part of Canada against another, I thought the time has come when we must forget this question of racial descent in this country and be Canadians first and foremost. I have felt for years that one of the things that may break down the fabric of this country is the fact that every ten years men who are and whose ancestors have been Canadians for generations have to register in the census their racial descent. That is one thing that perpetuates in this

country the type of citizenship that we do not want. I have no French blood in my veins, but I believe that those who do come from that part of Canada are as anxious and as willing to serve as those from any other part of this dominion and to assert the contrary is to do a great disservice to Canada and its unity of purpose.
Why all this talk about it? Why always cite Quebec?
Mention was made of that by the minister.

I beg my hon. friend's
pardon; the mention was first made by the hon. member for Parkdale.

I was replying to
the observations of the minister. The minister admits to-day something that we have said over and over again on this side of the house, that so far as this government is concerned there has been no concerted policy of recruiting. It has been spasmodic, and lackadaisical. He says-and I realize the load of responsibility he carries; have some appreciation of what it must be-that up to the present time we have not tried to get recruits in a large way. The result speaks for itself.
He gave the reasons.

In my opinion it
is due to the failure to have recruiting speeches and bands, but the consequence to-day is that this country is in a deadening torpor of complacency.
Oh, oh.

Hon. members can say what they wish. The reason why the minister says it is necessary for speeches on the part of members of parliament and others including the premier of Quebec is that the people have to be aroused now. Only a few days ago the minister made the statement in a speech that he delivered before the Rotary club in Toronto: "I think our most dangerous enemy on this side of the Atlantic is the idea that there is lots of time."
Too late, too late, has been the history of many countries in Europe to-day. We to-day have our Jena, our Austerlitz, we shall have our Waterloo if we realize before it is too late that something has to be done now to encourage recruiting, and to assure an ample production of the instruments of war, tanks aeroplanes and munitions.
The minister criticized the hon. member for Parkdale for some reference he made to there having been a failure in production. This is what the minister himself said-

I beg my hon. friend's
pardon; the only reference I made to the hon. member for Parkdale was in regard to his reference to a late senator. I mean the hon. member for Broadview.

The statement that the minister made as I understood it was this, that there had been no criticism of the Minister of Munitions and Supply in any statement that he made last night. The words of the minister were these:
He knows that our present commitments are for an army tank brigade, for a third division and for an armoured division. Those are the commitments we made for this year, and our endeavour naturally is to see to it that these units are supplied with equipment just as rapidly as possible. I cannot get equipment for these units any faster than Canadian industry turns it out.
Now after almost two years of war the minister of one department states in answer to the allegation made by the hon. member for York South, "What you say is true; there is not the equipment there should be; we have not been able to equip because industry has not produced." I ask the minister this: what about the National Resources Mobilization Act passed last June? It gave powers to this government asked by the Prime Minister as an emergency measure. It gave the government power to take over industries that were falling short. Why have the powers granted under this act not been utilized in order to ensure the required production? Yet we have been told repeatedly by the Minister of Munitions and Supply that all is well, that everything is in order, that tanks are being produced. Did the tank that was produced the other day have a Canadian engine or transmission? Then there is the question of aeroplane production, on which we have not had a report since March. We have had no report, nor have the people of Canada had a report, as to the present situation with regard to the production of aircraft. All we have had are general statements that all is well; and the psychological effect of the government continuously painting a picture of self-satisfaction in connection with Canada's war effort and the progress of the war has in the past engendered and will continue to engender apathy.
Why is there not the enlistment there should be? Look at the province of Saskatchewan, where we have a very fine record. Sometimes aspersions are levelled against those of racial descent other than British, but consider the record of the Ukrainian people and the contribution they have made and are making to our armed forces. If there is a failure to secure recruits it may be for one

of three reasons. The first is that so far as the various departments of this government are concerned there is no coordination. I am not going into any detail in that connection except to say that one of the strongest objections to recruiting has been the fact that the men in Canada did not receive fair treatment in the matter of transportation while on leave. The minister now has seen fit to remove that objection in large measure. Why was it not removed months ago? Six months ago the minister said it could not and would not be done.

Oh, no. If my hon. friend will permit me, what I said exactly was that free transportation could not be given. I stated that I would consult with the railways to see if there could be a reduction of fares; I did that, and that reduction has been made.
Mr. DIEFENBAIvER: Yes, Mr. Chairman, that was the last statement, after hon. members had brought up the matter time and again from June, 1940, on. It was postponed and put off. To-day that criticism has borne fruit. Why? Simply because of the fact that public opinion has been aroused and has demanded that something be done. One of the salient criticisms that I direct against this government to-day-and I say this in all kindliness-is that in many things it will not move until public opinion forces it to move.
Let me go back to the situation in Saskatchewan and western Canada generally. I have mentioned the wonderful record of the Ukrainian people and what I have said applies to Canadians of other racial descents in my province. One of the things most seriously hampering recruiting is the attitude that was taken by this government in an order in council passed on September 25, 1940, with regard to the Doukhobors. These people are antagonistic to any participation in warfare. Everyone, of course, respects religious scruples. The Doukhobors came to Canada, their rights being contained in an order in council dated December 6, 1898, which included the following paragraph with regard to military service:
The minister recommends that under the power vested in your excellency in council by the above provision, the Doukhobors, settling permanently in Canada, be exempted unconditionally, from service in the militia, upon the production in each case of a certificate of membership from the proper authorities of their community.
That was the exemption; that was the pledge upon which they settled in Canada. What happened in September, 1940? This government set up a higher type of citizenship for the Doukhobors in Saskatchewan and
British Columbia than is enjoyed by any British citizen in this dominion when it passed an order in council extending the order in council of 1898 to-
-the descendants of such immigrants who have continued without interruption to be members of the aforesaid sect or denomination . . .
The other day I was speaking to a Ukrainian who has two sons overseas with the forces of this country. He pointed out the situation in reference to the Doukhobors and said, "Nobody objects to their not having to fight in the armed forces of this country, but what did they do?" They refused to take their medical examinations when they were called up; they just did not turn up. Did the government punish any of them? And when the question of exemption was brought up they were ordered to appear before the military tribunal set up in the province of Saskatchewan, or at least they were ordered to appear along with all the others.
Not a military tribunal.
The tribunal headed by Hon. Mr. Justice Embury.
Not a military tribunal.
Then what do you call it?
The tribunal under the Department of National War Services.

That is it. Did they turn up when everybody else did? No. The Doukhobors said, "We will stay at home," and at home they stayed, and as yet they have not been proceeded against. This is what they said, according to the statement I have here: "We refuse to serve in any capacity. We will not leave our farms. We will refuse to appear for medical examination." The toleration of that sort of thing does not encourage recruiting. Why should these people, entitled as they are to exemption, be able to flaunt the laws of this country?
I have in my hands a copy of a letter written by the Doukhobors to the Prime Minister on June 24, 1940, which was attached to a return brought down the other day. In this letter the Doukhobors tell the Prime Minister what they are going to do in reference to the matter of military service. There is one paragraph in this letter which may afford an explanation for the unusually tender treatment being accorded these people, under which they are allowed to break the law at their own convenience.
You would no doubt recall that while on your election campaign the delegation of Named Doukhobors, consisting of Nilcoto Popoff, Alex

Cheveldave and others of Blaine Lake, Saskatchewan, have approached you at Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, on or about 29th day of February, regarding this same subject, and were assured by you that while there were no conscription of compulsory service required at that time, the issuance of such exemption certificates was unnecessary. And you have further assured them that the government would grant such exemption certificates to be issued in case the conscription or compulsory service would be necessary.
It was following this letter that the order in council was passed extending the order in council of 1898 to the descendants of those who entered this country at that time. The passing of the order in council has had a detrimental effect on recruiting in the province of Saskatchewan.
Let me give two other reasons. The first I pointed out the other day, and I am asking the minister to take it up with the Minister of Agriculture with a view to having it altered. In Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is in effect, under which the farmer must contribute one per cent of the value of his crop. Yet, Mr. Chairman, if any farmer who has contributed his proportion, as required by law, which assures him against failure in his crop, proceeds to enlist in the army of this country, between May 1 and November 1, he loses his bonus. Surely there is no justification for that. It is penalizing the man who enters Canada's army. We are asking for recruits across the country, in the agricultural districts as elsewhere. How can we ask for recruits if we say to a man who is prepared to leave his farm after sowing his crop, that if he enlists we will take away from him the right to share in the bonus provided by the government of Canada.
Surely that is inexcusable. It is an inexcusable detriment so far as recruiting in the agricultural districts is concerned.
I now pass on to the next matter.
What does my hon. friend mean by the -word "bonus"? He has said that the men will lose the bonus. What does he mean by that?

Quite a few farmers came back after the last war and took up land under the provisions of the Soldier Settlement Act. They have been farming ever since. They are in no better financial position than the general run of farmers, but from year to year they have continued to farm their land. Those men are re-enlisting in this war. What is happening to-day ? They leave behind them their dependents, their wives and children. Would hon. members not think that the department in charge of the administration of the Soldier Settlement Act would refrain from badgering those dependents at times such as these?
Let me explain. On March 19, 1941, this government passed an order in council providing as follows:
Notwithstanding any provision to the contrary contained in any of the regulations providing for payment of dependents' or marriage allowances in respect of dependents of members of the Canadian armed forces, that in all cases where the dependents of an enlisted person continue to occupy the farm for which such person is indebted to the director of soldier settlement and in respect of which the contract terms are not otherwise satisfactorily provided for, there may be deducted from the dependents' or marriage allowance amounts sufficient to provide for payment of taxes-
And so on. What an invitation to enlist! Those people go overseas, and this is the way they are treated. I have letters here-one from a man who left his wife and two children on the land. He is advised by the department-I should say that she is advised-that $15 a month is to be deducted from her allowance in order to pay taxes against land owned by the government of Canada. A portion of the letter she received from the department of dependents' allowances reads:
It is felt that in your own interests and those of your husband this financial provision is essential in order that the debt against your home and farm will not amount to proportions beyond the capacity of the farm to carry.
In effect the department informs her: "Your husband is in the army. You are not going to get the dependents' allowance that others get. You are not to get it, because your husband owes money to the soldier settlement board. We are going to deduct from the allowances made to you."
As taxes.

Yes. Here is the
explanation-so that the land will not be lost.

We on this side of the house are not trying to create difficulties for the government. We are pointing out these things with a view to having them remedied. Hon. gentlemen may have read Ambassador Bullitt's speech the other day in which he said that 5,000 tanks and aeroplanes would have spelled the difference between victory and defeat for France. Just a few more men-

speechtext: They had the men.

They had men dispersed in various parts of the world and men who were lulled into a false sense of security behind what they thought was an impregna-able line, the Maginot line, just as some
people in Canada think we have an impregnable line for the defence of Canada, in the Atlantic ocean, and apathy was the result.
I place this matter before the committee, Mr. Chairman, with a view to having this injustice remedied, so that we shall be able to secure that enthusiasm which is necessary if we are to overcome the apathy of the last few months engendered as a result of the failure, as I see it, on the part of those in authority to make the people of Canada realize the need and the danger and awfulness of the prospect that faces us unless Canada acts now.

Mr. Chairman, some time later in the day, or perhaps some time tomorrow, the Canadian parliament will adjourn, and apparently the intention is that it may not meet again for a period of approximately five months. During that time anything may happen in this world. Those five months will be the most critical five months in the history of civilization, and as a member of this parliament representing a great riding on the Pacific coast I feel that it is my duty to bring to the attention of the house before we adjourn certain suggestions and criticisms in connection with our war effort.
May I say at the outset that I listened this morning with great interest to the statement of the Prime Minister. I was very much concerned about certain portions of that statement and about the attitude of the leader of Canada, because it seemed to me that he was satisfied with Canada's war effort. I wish most heartily that I could convince myself that he is right, because it would be a great relief to me. But I cannot do so, and I do not believe that the Canadian people are satisfied that Canada is doing everything that can be done. They ask for nothing less. They insist on having that much. There is uneasiness, there is misgiving across this nation to-day, and may I point out some of the things which I think are wrong in connection with our war effort, some of the things which need to be remedied and need to be remedied without further delay.
In the first place we have too few men in Great Britain, too few men in the battle line. There are two battle lines in this war, one in Great Britain and one in the Mediterranean. Our battle line is in Great Britain, and I do not quarrel with such disposition of our troops, for Great Britain is probably the best place they could serve. Canada's battle line is in Great Britain, as every member of this house well knows, and the time of battle is in this year 1941, not in 1942 or 1943, or five years hence. The hour of Canada's battle comes this year. Yet what do we find?
Supply-National Defence

We find that there are brave Canadians in Great Britain, two infantry divisions and corps troops as well as the men serving in the navy and the air force. We find at home here in Canada, thousands of miles from our battle line, two more infantry divisions, and an armoured division and a tank brigade, made up of equally brave men, men who have been recruited, most of them, for over a year; some of them have been on active service for nearly two years-men who are without exception keen to do one thing and one thing only, and that is to get to Great Britain to fight.
It is clear-I do not think this can be contradicted-that these men can receive their final training and their full equipment only after they arrive in Great Britain. They cannot get these things here in Canada. It is equally clear that if they were sent to Great Britain it would be a spur to recruiting in Canada. Nothing would make it easier to get recruits in Canada. It is clear also that sending them to Great Britain would improve the morale of the troops themselves, and it is obvious that Great Britain needs every fighting man she can get. Our motherland has had to call up men in their late thirties. We find this statement made in April by a leading British general; I quote from the Vancouver Sun of April 15, from a Canadian Press dispatch:
London, April 15.-Lieutenant-General Sir Wilfrid Lindsell, in charge of administration, home forces, indicated to-day that the war office is ready to equip the Canadian tank brigade when it comes to England to join the Canadian corps.
"The more divisions of Canadians to arrive here the better," General Lindsell declared.
The more divisions we can send the better, and my hon. friend knows as well as anybody why they are not going faster.
No, that is one thing your hon. friend does not know. I cannot understand why portions at least of these divisions have not been sent over to England long before this.
If my hon. friend will think twice he can imagine the reason. He knows the demands on shipping around the cape in the last three months.
I sometimes wonder whether the wish, whether the desire to get fighting men to England from Canada is as strong as some people would have us believe.
It is as strong as I could wish.

In January of this year the Minister of National Defence announced to Canada that Canada's commitment for this

year would be a third division, an armoured division, and a tank brigade, and he said again yesterday that that was Canada's commitment for the year. I could not understand the way in which he used that word "commitment." Surely the position is such that if Canada's commitment for this year is too small, it may be too small for all time. We may be wiped out in this country. Things have happened since last January. Let us review our commitment in the light of events which have taken place since then. The year is almost half over, and yet none of these troops have gone to Great Britain. I say to the government that they should be sent over just as quickly as possible and that the fourth division should also be sent to Great Britain instead of being kept in Canada on what might be called home guard duties.
The second point that I wish to place before the minister is this. I believe that the fighting departments, the navy, the army and the air force, are not adapting themselves to modern warfare as quickly as they should. One has the feeling that the Department of National Defence has become departmentalized into three channels-navy, army and air channels. Things have been happening recently in Europe, particularly in Greece and in Crete, and I suggest that we should set up in our defence department a small war council to direct the whole military effort of Canada, having in mind all arms of the service.
For example, why should we not raise air divisions in Canada such as the Germans used with such success in Crete? I understand that they are smaller in personnel than the ordinary infantry division. Why should we not train such troops in Canada? Let us build up air divisions which could be used in the forefront of the battle when the time comes to take the offensive. The men could be trained here in Canada much more easily than in Great Britain, where they would be subject to attack by enemy bomber and fighter planes. No arm of the service would be so likely to attract recruits as air divisions, and such divisions would be invaluable not only overseas but during the time of their training here for the defence of Canada should it be necessary to defend Canadian territory.
I suggest also that full scope is not being given to Canadian initiative. One of the greatest assets of the Canadian man and the Canadian woman is his and her initiative, and I suggest that that quality should be used to the full at this time; let us make more use of the initiative of those in civilian life, of our citizen soldiers, and of course of Canadians in the permanent force. Let us not in all these

In the third place, I suggest that the ministry are not facing the facts about manpower. I do not wish to say anything which will hurt the minister's recruiting campaign-
It is not mine. It is the campaign of Canada.

Well, the recruiting campaign of Canada. As the minister knows already, I have offered to help him in any way I can. But there is this fact to consider. This is not the only recruiting campaign which will be carried on. It will be necessary continuously to raise recruits, and are we to take it that the minister will object indefinitely, or until the end of the war, to anything that may be said which might be considered as affecting adversely his recruiting campaigns? Speaking on this subject, the minister told us on June 5, as reported in Hansard, page 3534:
I have every reason to believe that, with the acceleration which has taken place in the campaign, and with the assurances we have received, the campaign will be a complete success.
Now that, Mr. Chairman, is soothing the Canadian people; I do not think it is putting the facts squarely before them. It is a mistake for the minister to make statements of that kind. May I cite a statement made by Major-General Alexander, officer commanding the Pacific command, as reported in the Vancouver papers on May 31. It is a call for volunteers, and begins as follows:
An urgent call for volunteers for the Canadian active army was issued to-day by Major-General R. O. Alexander, general officer commanding-in-chief, Pacific command.
In his statement General Alexander used these words:
A special recruiting campaign is now being carried on from coast to coast. The result of this campaign in this district, to date, has been far below the actual and urgent need.
That statement was confirmed on June 7, six days ago, in an editorial in the Vancouver Sun which, as the minister knows, is a strong supporter of the government-

latitude, but certainly it would be against all the recognized rules of debate in the house to continue much longer any more than the briefest references to statements in the press. I wish merely to read three short paragraphs from this editorial, because it shows the position with regard to recruiting on the Pacific coast. It says:
Recruiting has fallen down in this province. There is no use blinking the fact. We have got to face it, and see what must be done about it. The army wants 32,000 men from all Canada, 3,100 of them from British Columbia. Mr. Ralston told the House of Commons this week they had about one-quarter the needed number.
When Mr. Ralston says this is "satisfactory" we wonder where he gets his complacency. The drive has been on since May 11, and is scheduled to finish at the end of June.
In British Columbia they have still to get 2,445 men between now and the end of the month. In four days of this month they added only 91 men.
I suggest to the minister that he would be more likely to get recruits if he placed that position squarely before the Canadian people. Do not let them believe that this recruiting campaign is going well if it is not.
There are reasons why the campaign is not going well, and I believe they should be pondered by the government, particularly in view of the fact that further recruits will be called for from time to time.
One unfavourable circumstance, of course, is the failure to use the enthusiasm of young Canadians which manifested itself so clearly when the war broke out. This is ancient history, and I do not intend to say anything with regard thereto except this, that it has engendered in the minds of many of these young men the attitude, "Oh, they would not take me when I was willing to go, now they can come and get me." One encounters that feeling time and time again in talking to these young men. There is no lack of courage among them. I think we must be most careful not to accuse them of lack of courage, no matter from what part of Canada they come or from what race they spring.
Another point which is worrying them is the inequality of sacrifice. Here is a young man in a job; he is willing to enlist; he enlists; another young man comes and takes over his job. There is that possibility always present in the minds of these men. An

employer who operates big logging camps on the Queen Charlotte islands, writing me a few days ago, pointed out this fact. He said:
Take for instance, our own operation on the Queen Charlotte islands; eighty-five per cent of our crew is now composed of foreigners; most of them are not naturalized. These men are taking the places of young Canadians who are to a great extent being used as home guards.
That is the position which the minister has to face.
Then, let the government not forget that it took over the direction of the young man power of Canada when it brought in compulsory training. Now the tendency of these young men is to wait for a lead. They wait for the government to say what is to be done next. Our whole way of living has changed since the last war. We are subject to government direction in many, many more ways than we were at that time. That is another reason why these young men are waiting,-waiting to be directed into whatever channel they are required to go, waiting for action by the government. I am convinced that the government must face the possibility, and face it now, that it will have to decide who is to serve, and how. That applies not only to the men but to the women. Eventually we shall have to put every man and woman in this country in his or her proper place in this war effort, and the government has to accept the responsibility for making the decisions with regard to who goes where.
Another reason why these young men have not been enlisting is the treatment given to men already in the forces. I hate to say this, but I must, because I believe it is true and is important. It may be that the cause has been the great rush of events; there have been so many things to do. But in this war, far more even than in the last, Canada must go to any length to see that the men of her fighting forces are properly treated. Only in that way can she get volunteers in adequate numbers in this war.
Take for example the question of dependents' allowances. I find in Saturday Night of May 31, 1941, a full-page advertisement calling for recruits:
Step up and step out in a uniform!
Down below are these words:
You are needed now for active service.
Rates of pay in the ranks.
The rates of pay are set out, and then we read this:
Dependent allowances in cash: $35 to wife, $12 each per month for 2 children-only 3 dependents per soldier.
[Mr. Green.1
That decision was made at the beginning of the war because Canada did not want men with-more than two children to enlist. Men who had more than two children did enlist, but they have never been able to get allowances for more than the two. Now we are calling for any Canadian and every Canadian to enlist, and yet men with three or four children can get only an allowance for two. That is an unfair situation, it is one which will hamper recruiting, and it should be remedied without further delay.
A week or two ago there was an argument in this house about pensions. In the last war any man who enlisted was covered by what was known as the insurance principle of pensions, or the "incurred on" principle. In other words, if he incurred disability on service, even here in Canada, he got a pension. In this war that has been greatly modified. It was wiped out for a year, from some date in May last year until a few weeks ago, in so far as the men serving in Canada were concerned. However, within the last two weeks some change has been made, as was announced in the house. But we did not go the full length, we did not make that insurance principle applicable to the men who are going to England to do the fighting for us. Things like that hamper recruiting.
Again, vi'e have not to-day provision in Canada for reconditioning the men who are discharged from the forces. A man comes back with a stomach ulcer and is discharged. If he is in need of active remedial treatment he can get treatment in a pension hospital for the period of a year. But as between the man who can qualify and the man who is put out of the army but is yet not really fit to go to work, there is a large gap. Canada should set up some sort of reconditioning depots or convalescent camps, so that these men can be nursed back to health. In many cases they could be put back into the forces, not perhaps to go overseas, but to relieve other men who are fit to go overseas.
Further, we have not yet decided whether the privileges of land settlement will be extended to the men of the present forces, or whether they will be able to get soldier insurance. Those two matters should be considered right away and, in my opinion, put into operation. They would provide just that much more attraction to the men we wish to enlist.
Finally, members of this government may not like this, but I believe it is true-the general attitude of this Canadian government is wrong, because it is moved as the result of its fears. An outstanding example of that is what it has done recently with regard to

wheat for Japan. Time and again this government moves because it is afraid of something, or more afraid of something else. That is an attitude which is entirely out of line with the courage of the Canadian people. They are calling at this time for fighting leadership, and to fighting leadership they are entitled. Right Hon. Winston Churchill said a day or two ago in London, at a gathering of dominion and allied representatives:
But here also, duly authorized by the parliament and democracy of Britain, are gathered the servants of the ancient British monarchy and accredited representatives of the British dominions beyond the seas, of Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, of the empire of India, of Burma, and of our colonies in every quarter of the globe. They have drawn their swords in this cause. They will never let them fall till life is gone or victory is won.
Till life is gone or victory is won. That is wnat the Canadian people face to-day. I plead with the government to announce as our war aim the smashing of Germany. Let it be as simple as that-that we are out to smash Germany-and let this government give bold and tough leadership. If it will do that, the Canadian people will rush to follow.

I had not intended to say anything in this debate, particularly since we have reached the last stage of this part of the session, and especially since we are discussing estimates; but as I listened to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) I began to realize some of the reasons why there is not a better response to the efforts that are being made for recruiting than we have been having in the last little while.
I am decidedly of the opinion that the hearts of the people of Canada have not yet been properly touched with what this war means to us. Every now and then I ask myself why that is, and I am afraid I have found the answer during the last ten or fifteen minutes.
Let us go back and see what has taken place during the time that we, the elected representatives of the people of Canada, have been sitting in this House of Commons. There is a recruiting campaign going on, and very much depends upon the success or failure of that campaign. I am certainly hoping it will be a success. I believe that hon. members who have been speaking also share that hope. But what is going to be the result if it is a failure? How long has this house been in session? What have we been doing that is of importance to the war effort during the many months that we have been sitting in this chamber? The hon. member for Vancouver South said that he had told the Minister of National Defence that he was willing to do 14873-250
everything he could to help to make the campaign for recruits a success. Of course, he is willing to help; he is anxious to do what every hon. member in this house wishes to do, and has probably made an effort to help the Minister of National Defence. He read extracts from newspapers to indicate that if the campaign is going to succeed it must succeed during the month of June. Why was not some effort made to permit the members of the house to get away, at an earlier date, from this portion of our parliamentary duties so that we could assist the Minister of National Defence in making the campaign a success? I challenge any member of the house to look over the records during the last six or eight weeks and find more than ten per cent of what has taken place to have been of benefit to the war effort of Canada.
I know that when I say that, if it should be reported, I am perhaps helping to bring down the level of this institution of parliament in public opinion. But what I say is true. As I listened to the hon. member, he told us of some of the causes of the lack of response on the part of the young men of Canada to the appeal to engage themselves by voluntary effort in this war, which is a war of Canada's, just as much as it is a war of the people of the British isles or of any other part of the world. But did he appeal to the young men of Canada to put aside the sense of injustice to which he made reference and to enlist anyway because of the gravity of the situation?
I am talking to the old men of Canada to-day, I am afraid.

Very well. But what the hon. member has said to-day is, after all, only a repetition of what has been said in this house practically since the beginning of the war. The hon. gentleman read extracts from newspapers. These same newspapers time after time have devoted all their energy to creating disaffection in the young men of Canada toward those who are in the armed forces and those who have not yet enlisted. Unfortunately that is what a good many of us have been doing in this House of Commons. Effort after effort has been made to destroy the confidence of the people, old men and young men, women and children of Canada, in the government that is charged with the responsibility of carrying on this war. To-day, some people not being satisfied with trying to destroy confidence in the ministers themselves, there appears to be taking place an effort to destroy confidence even in the military men who are at the head of the armed forces of Canada. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, and through you every hon. member wherever he may sit, can we induce young

Supply-National Defence

men. to enlist on a voluntary basis by continually trying to destroy confidence in the men who are going to lead them, by continually referring to the injustices that without question have been heaped upon the men who suffered from the last war? We must do more than call the attention of the men and women of Canada to things that some of us think to be unjust. In addition to that, we must show them that in spite of anything that may have the appearance of injustice and, in fact, be unjust, it is their duty first of all to assist Canada when this, their country, is in distress, and second, we should show them on every possible occasion that if they do not assist Canada to-day, then Canada will not be able to assist in saving the world from the fate that is threatening it at this moment.
Another cause for the lack of response is, I understand, this. We have heard expressions in this house, and echoes of these expressions in the country at large, and it has struck me that unfortunately many men, leading men who have set ideas are thinking more of the particular idea that they have in mind than of making a serious effort to help in the winning of the war. For instance, there are very many who are strongly in favour of conscription, in opposition to the voluntary system. I am taking no exception whatever to those who wish for conscription, and when I make the general statement which I am about to make I do not say that it includes every person who is in favour of conscription. But I ask hon. members, is there not a tendency on the part of those men and women of Canada who want conscription to place all their energies behind a campaign to bring about conscription rather than to place those energies behind a campaign to make the war effort of Canada stronger and better and more successful than it is to-day? The same thing is true of those whose main idea centres round questions of social progress and reform. Is there not a tendency on their part, or on the part of many of them, to place all their energies behind a campaign to bring about more and more rapid social progress rather than to direct their energies towards accelerating the speed of Canada's war effort?
Turn back to what I said about the records of this house. I have wondered why we were not released long ago to go out and help the ministry of defence in getting recruits. I said that if hon. members would look back over the last six weeks, they would not find more than 10 per cent of the record of the doings from day to day of this house devoted entirely to the effort to win the war. What is more, I venture to say it would be

found that nearly 50 per cent of the debates in this house consist of repetitions, restatements, of what has already been said by some other hon. member, repetition of question after question, each question dealing with something that has already been answered. We who represent the people of Canada would have been doing far more service to Canada, to Great Britain, to the British empire and to all who are allied with us if we had been out in the country, each where he thinks he can do the most good, making, first, an appeal for recruits and, second, trying to convince the people of what every one of us believes to be true, namely, that whatever injustices have been allowed to germinate and grow in the past are soon going to be uprooted. We; who sit here, no matter on which side of the house we sit, know that as a result of this war and the efforts being made in connection with it, there is going to be a greater measure of social progress in the next few years than there has been during a century in any country of the world. We know that; why can we not each one go to the country and convince the people who listen to us of what is taking place, that they should not lose hope of a greater measure of justice than was given to the men who enlisted and fought for us in the last war. Let us try to make them see, notwithstanding some of the disaffections which naturally are theirs to-day, that the only way to reach that state of social progress .is to make certain that Canada and those associated with Canada win this war, and that the only way in which Canada can win the war is to have her people more deeply touched with the necessity of winning it than they are to-day.
I rose to speak not for the purpose of chastising but rather for the purpose of suggesting that from now on we should stop trying to destroy confidence in our leaders both civil and military, stop trying to destroy confidence in the determination of the people of Canada, and set ourselves to restore that confidence and try to impress upon them the necessity of realizing that although mistakes may have been made they should join the colours and do everything they can to have Canada carry on a greater and more stupendous war effort even than she has been doing in the past.
With that hope I take my seat. I trust we shall not be here much longer, and I sincerely hope that when we return in the summer or the fall we shall devote ourselves with all our capacity and ability and energy to trying to create, always to create, a greater war effort and not to destroying confidence in our military and civil leaders.
