Members of this house are entitled to know just what kind of policy has been urged upon this country by the Bank of England. I say that the governor of the Bank of England has proved himself to be a traitor, and I believe that all association with this bank, so far as Canada is concerned, should be cut off.
I do not consider that Germany's successes have been achieved on the field of battle alone. I think Germany's successes have been very largely due to acts of treachery committed by people in high places in various allied countries. We know that happened in Norway; we know it happened in France. I am suggesting that it has happened and is happening in England, and I am wondering to what extent it is happening in Canada to-day. There are many things in this country that people cannot understand. As the hon. member for Battle River stated the other day, there are brakes on our war effort. We think those brakes should be removed, and should have beeD removed a long time ago. We all know that from September, 1939, to May, 1940, we slumbered. Apparently we felt that we were safe so long as the Maginot line remained, but after May, 1940, we suddenly realized that it was necessary to wake up. But it is impossible for a country to wake up immediately and develop at once a fighting force ready to go overseas. Now we are told that *one reason why we cannot expand our production at a greater rate is the lack of skilled labour. The other day I made the statement that we should do the same with labour as we have done in connection with the army. We do not refuse to take men into the army on the ground that they are not skilled, although the soldier of to-day has become a highly skilled man. We take men into the army and train them, and I maintain that we should do exactly the same so far as industry is concerned. We should take unskilled people and give them the necessary training to enable them to take their places in industry. The other day the hon. member for Essex East asked if I was aware of the fact that we were training or had trained in the neighbourhood of fifty thousand men, but those men were not trained to the point that when they finished their training they were able to go into industry. What we lack to-day is a link between the schools and industry; in other words, we need schools to give advanced training. In the United States they have schools that provide such training, but so far as I know, there is only one such school in Canada, namely, in British Columbia.

The other day we were discussing this question in the pensions committee, and it was admitted that in the west there is a very long list of people waiting for training. Many people are trying to get into those schools in the west, but there is no room for them. So far as the east is concerned, they seem to be actually short of applicants. I suggested that we might well move some of the people from the west to the schools of the east, but I was told that it would be an expensive business. Then I suggested that we might put more schools into operation in the west in order to give these people the training they want, but I was told that then we would be training more men than industry could absorb. Yet in this chamber we had been told by the Minister of Munitions and Supply that we had a shortage of skilled labour. One of those statements cannot be true. If industry cannot expand because we have not skilled labour, then we want more skilled labour. If we want more skilled labour, then we should equip more schools in the west to train those men. Yet we are told that there is no use in having more schools, because we would be putting men into the labour market who could not find jobs. Those are questions which people are asking. A situation like that will do more harm to our war effort than will any other situation of which I could conceive. For this government to say that they are doing everything in their power to expand the war effort, while there are thousands of people throughout Canada looking for jobs, just does not make sense.
I did not intend taking the time of the committee further, because I know it is the desire to close down either to-night or tomorrow. For this reason I shall not speak at greater length. I suggest to the minister, however, that if we do not do anything else at this time to expand industry, we should at least put into operation advanced training schools which will take up that slack between the state of a man's training after he comes out of the training schools, and the state of training required by industry-one of skilled labour.

As one of those who have been in some way entrusted with a certain degree of responsibility for the success of the recruiting drive, I believe it my duty to mention certain conditions which I have observed and believe to be general in that part of Canada in which I live. These are circumstances of which I have learned while in contact with troops and officers from all parts of Canada.
There can be no doubt that those who are charged with the recruiting effort to-day are

Supply-National Defence
doing everything humanly possible to get recruits. In the metropolitan area of the city of Toronto, alone, we have fifty recruiting stations. The officers entrusted with this grave task have worked zealously day and night. So far as possible we have enlisted the services of patriotic civilians. The work has never flagged. I disagree, however, with the minister's statement with regard to national service. I am not advocating anything; it is not my duty to advocate. But I believe, and I believe this in absolute sincerity, that a national service act would not disrupt the country, but rather would unite it.
I believe the Canadian people are looking anxiously for some such act, some such move. That is my opinion. I have seen, and talked with officers and men in the army, with civilians, with youngsters coming out of school, and I believe they would welcome it. If this government finds it necessary to enact such a measure, I make this pledge, that so long as I am in the public life of this dominion I shall never use the discomfiture of the government, if they have to bring in national service, for political purposes: Had this been done ever since the last war there would have been no talk of racial disunity in Canada to-day. That is all I have to say with regard to compulsory national service.
I know the recruiting figures; I see them every day. I am naturally not allowed to mention them in this house, but I can say that we need men and that the need is imperative. It has not been impressed on the country how badly we do need men, and that we need the best men we can possibly get for the army. The man in the army to-day, particularly in the armoured formations, has to be a better mechanic, a better signaller, a better craftsman, a better tradesman than the man in the factory. We want the best in the army. The man in the army must be prepared to do all the things that a man in industry must do. He must be prepared to do them in the most frightful discomfort and he must be prepared to do them twice as fast and in shocking working conditions. I do not believe that we have stressed the vital need for the best we have in Canada for the army to-day.
The army is the highest of the professions in Canada at the present time. I notice that there is a certain bitterness about the war effort, a bitterness which is growing. The Globe and Mail of Toronto had an editorial this morning which would repay everyone's reading. It says that civilian morale is bad. There can be no question about the justification of that editorial. Civilian morale is bad all across Canada because we have not had from the beginning that candour, that downright leadership which we must expect. It
should be a great thing to be a Canadian. People are now going round as if it were a disgrace, but it is a great thing to be a Canadian. We are a great country. Let us see to it that our effort is put out in this war and that the name of Canada will remain gallantly at the masthead.
With regard to national service, I should like to quote from an article by General Wavell. I will be brief, but I think there is a message in it for us. He said:
The soldier is apt^ to disregard or underrate the statesman's difficulties. I remember one of our present politicians giving an apt illustration of this tendency. He instanced a soldier's impatience at the slowness of the statesman to implement some political measure which was agreed to be essential, say compulsory service. If you agree it has to be done, why not do it at once? says the soldier. The politician might retort thus: When you come to a river line defended by the enemy, which you must cross to reach your objective, do you assault it forthwith? Of course not, the soldier will reply; it is essential to reconnoitre, to group the artillery, to construct bridges, to draw the enemy's attention away from the point of crossing, and so on. Just so, says the politician, so must I prepare public opinion, anticipate objections, draw up a measure which will be fair to all classes, arrange for the medical examination of men liable, decide on exemptions, and so forth.
That article has a great message for us in Canada to-day.
With regard to man-power, had we been able to have a division in Libya it is altogether probable that to-day we would still occupy Libya. We have recently been told by Mr. Churchill that the army of the Nile consisted of a mere two divisions, so that we can see how desperate the need is for man-power and machines. These are matters that must be brought home to the Canadian people. We are all in this war, every single one of us. Another division in the near east might have entirely averted the threat to Suez. I do not believe for an instant that Suez will fall, but I believe we must have more men for the near east, and I believe the Canadian troops are the most mechanically minded in the British empire. I see in the headlines of the papers to-night that Vichy reports that Canadian troops are already in Syria. May I ask the minister whether there is any truth in that statement. Is he prepared to make a statement, or is it a matter on which he cannot speak?
That is all I wanted to say, but I wish to impress upon the committee that what we must do, all of us, is to go out and get our pride back, for it is a great thing to be a Canadian. We are a great country, and we are not going to get our pride back by stopping criticism. We are not going to do it by innuendo. Talk about racial differences, as if we were a split country, must
Supply-National Defence

stop. We must be a united country, and I believe we are. I believe we are capable of going ahead, and it is up to the government to give the lead. The country is with the government, but it is demanding action. I am absolutely convinced that no matter what measures may be brought down, the government will find no difficulty from the Canadian people. But they will find grave and serious difficulty, even peril, if things continue as they are and Canadians continue to believe that the government is not prosecuting this war with an all-out 100 per cent total effort.

I was tempted to rise because of a statement made across the floor. It was said that some of our difficulties at this time were due to the fact that men were trying to stress and to press for social reforms that were not called for. Another hon. gentleman to my right makes the statement that Canada, when she moved for the compulsory training of the youth of the country, indicated that she had taken a step in the direction of conscription. I do not agree with these statements. Most of the discussion this afternoon I would construe as an attempt to force the government on the question of conscription. For the past two months, listening to the different ministers reporting to the house on the activities of their respective departments, I have become convinced that it is not man-power of which Canada is short and that there is absolutely no necessity at this time to talk about the conscription of manpower.
We have in Canada to-day under arms and in training camps many more men than we are capable of equipping. I would also call the attention of the hon. gentleman who suggests that military training is now compulsory in Canada, to the fact that when we passed the mobilization act we gave the government power to mobilize the whole financial and industrial resources of the country; and if there is need at this time for conscription of anything, it is conscription of the resources of the country to manufacture the necessary arms to equip the men who are in our camps already. In my part of the dominion I do not think there is any difficulty in securing recruits, because a large percentage of the men who are employed in the coal mines at all events, are only too anxious to get into the army; for leaving the coal mine to go to war is a vacation to them. I think the recruiting officers will find that that is the situation there.
We can make speeches in the house until further orders, but all the oratory in the world is not going to cure the situation. We must do something about the causes that

affect the war situation generally. In addressing myself to the Minister of National Defence I am not going to deal with production and other matters which have nothing to do with his department, but I should like to bring to his attention one or two things which I believe have an adverse effect on the morale of our army particularly, and on the men who are going into training at the present time. Complaint after complaint is made that men who have enlisted for military training and are paid $1.30 a day go into the training camps and are put to work on national defence construction projects, in the erection of huts and so forth in the camp, replacing the ordinary labour which should be employed on such work. The result is that the men who have enlisted for military training find themselves doing carpenter's work or plumber's work or some other form of labour which should be done by men outside the army who are dependent for their livelihood on these particular lines of work.
I would call the minister's attention to a brief which was prepared by local union 1588 in Sydney, of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America. The local union has a membership of five or six hundred, and in this brief they complain specifically of the erection of huts by enlisted men. That is not good for the army itself. The man in uniform does not want that kind of work; it is not good for recruiting, because those who would join up for military training see the men in the camps engaged in that kind of work, and it is not good for labour to have men in uniform doing the work at a lower wage than is paid outside for such labour. This brief speaks very strongly against soldiers being used on any national defence project where there is a labour supply available, as there is in Sydney. It gives many instances where work of this kind has been done by men in uniform, and if the minister has not a copy of the brief I think he should familiarize himself with its contents. As I say, this sort of thing is bad both for the potential soldier and for the soldier himself, and if it is being carried on right across Canada in community after community, we can all appreciate what the effect will be.
Some hon. gentleman has made the suggestion here that the services of each and every individual who belongs to any of the services at this time should be fully utilized on the basis of his experience, that he should be placed in a position where he can make his maximum contribution. I agree heartily with that statement.
I would call specifically to the minister's attention the case of a young man who came over here from the United States, as many

Supply-National Dejence
are doing at the present time, in order to enlist. He left a good job in his own country, being sufficiently interested in the principles for which Canada has engaged in this war. He is a newspaper correspondent who has been all over the world, knows the international situation thoroughly, and was prepared to make a contribution in his own field. It is some ten months since he came to Ottawa and offered his services. He was advised at that time that the way in which he could make his best contribution would be to get into the army. He enlisted as a private soldier and has been at the depot since then in that capacity.
He started in to make a valuable contribution to the army. I believe that if there are any people in Canada whose morale must be built up, it is the young men who have enlisted in Canada's forces. In a great many instances Canada has not been very good to them in the past, and there is no doubt that most of them are coming into the army in a bad frame of mind. This young man undertook the responsibility of issuing a magazine. He published biographical sketches of the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, and carried on a line of education-I would not call it propaganda- for the benefit of the troops from camp to camp. What cooperation did he receive? From the beginning he had to turn out that magazine from his own pay of $39 a month. He continued that work until last month, by which time he had gone so far in the red that he had to discontinue it. He got no financial assistance from anybody; he rented a typewriter at his own expense, bought his own stencils, and did all the work himself. He has tried every way he can to get into the field wherein he has specialized. I should have thought that a United States newspaper correspondent with contacts all over his own country and with credentials from some of the most influential people there could have been fully utilized in offsetting the influences of Lindbergh and the isolationist groups in the United States. But that was not done, and this young man to-day is in a frame of mind that he wants to be discharged. If the minister is not aware of the case of which I have spoken, I shall be glad to give him the information privately. I do not care to broadcast these things. I have talked on several occasions to this young man and am convinced that he is all he appears to be. I have confirmed my opinion by reference to the mounted police, who inform me that there is no suspicion of his bona fides, and that his credentials are in order. I do not know why, at this time, when a man of this
type volunteers his services, we cannot undertake to place him and those like him where they can make their maximum contribution in influencing United States opinion on behalf of our cause.
Our recruiting campaign, I understand, is somewhat slack in this city. A young man of this type, whose services have not been utilized, and whose treatment may become more widely known, will not have a very good influence on recruiting.
Talking will not cure the conditions to which I have referred. Something must be done. I believe that the Minister of National Defence must accept in the present emergency more responsibility with respect to direction. The government will have to cut through the line of red tape which has been the system for the last twenty or thirty years. It would take one six weeks to put an order through from the Jackson building and to have it finally O.-K-ed and ratified, and that is not good enough to-day. The minister himself must make an investigation-and he is capable of doing so-into what is necessary at this time for the promotion of the best interests of the country in the administration of the department, instead of having the system of pigeon-holes, putting a thing into one pigeonhole after another, as in the past. He should issue orders directly and have them carried out. He must cut through the maze of red tape which I know exists, has always existed and will always exist until someone is big enough to accept responsibility and will stand up and recognize the emergency, brushing away everything that is irrelevant.

I resent the remarks of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Turgeon) and those of the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald), delivered the other day. Both these gentlemen said the same thing-that we on this side of the house were endeavouring to undermine the confidence of the people of Canada in this government. I do not think either of these gentlemen should have made that statement. They are not right in saying it. Certainly the last thing we have in mind is undermining the confidence of the Canadian people in the government. We have already, on many occasions, offered our cooperation with the government, and they are getting it to-day for the sake of Canada's war effort.
There are many apparently minor matters, however, that mean a great deal to the enthusiasm of the people for a greater effort in connection with the war. For example, I would call the attention of the committee to something that has had a bad effect. Yesterday, a man who has been an outstanding personality in Canada, an eminent Prime
Supply-National Defence

Minister of the country-I refer to the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett as he was then-had a very high honour bestowed upon him by His Majesty the King, and it seems to me it was rather small of us not to show some public recognition of that fact on the floor of the house. With other members of the House of Commons, I cabled my congratulations, but I do think that this honour, conferred upon a great Canadian, should have been recognized from the floor of the house. I have received several telegrams from different people who are very much upset over the manner in which that honour was recognized.
Let me assure the government that we are not criticizing without reason. I have listened to a good deal of criticism to-day, and I think it is good for the government that there should be such criticism. To go back to the earlier days of the war, had it not been for the prodding we gave the government, a good many things that have been corrected would have been left untouched. I know it has happened. Let me call the attention of the committee to the words of Mr. Menzies. He said that the people of Australia had said to him: "You go ahead; you lead this country." I say that to the government: "You lead this country, but lead it, and if you go too slow we will prod you." There is no reason, however, why we should be subject to abuse for doing the prodding in a constructive way in an endeavour to secure a better war effort and to have certain things that are not right remedied. I will go further and say, in the words of Mr. Menzies, "If jmu go too fast we shall be delighted, because we did not expect it of you." That is the attitude which I feel should be taken. In my opinion, I repeat, some recognition should have been given the honour conferred upon Mr. Bennett. I do not see any difference between a man receiving a degree from a university, honoris causa, and receiving an honour from the king for meritorious work. The only difference is that the fatter comes from a higher and greater power than a university. It is unfortunate that the honour to Mr. Bennett was not betteT recognized, because what has happened has had a disturbing effect upon a good many people.
I asked the minister yesterday for the figures of the men discharged from the forces from the beginning of the war. Has he them to-day?

All discharges to the 31st of May were 32,461, all ranks, including 473 discharged overseas. The number of those returned from overseas and discharged is 1,658. The break-down is, medically unfit, 60 per cent -these are rough percentages-under age,

irregular enlistment, 6 per cent; not likely to become efficient, or misconduct, 24 per cent; the note says that the larger number of these took place in the early days of the war. The recent regulations have reduced the number discharged for these causes. The percentage of those transferred to other services is 3 per cent; those discharged for miscellaneous reasons, including compassionate grounds, to resume civil occupation, et cetera, 7 per cent.
At what rate are they being discharged each month?
Up to May the number was 1.912.
Per month?
Monthly average for five months.

What is being done
in the department with regard to women's organizations? The department should take some definite stand and give some assistance to these organizations, which are being developed across Canada, They are useful to the country, and I think we should know something of what they are doing.

That is something with regard to which I expected the former Minister of National War Services would have made a statement, but owing to the change in portfolio this has been left to his successor. The whole matter of the organization, or of interest in the organization, of women is a much larger subject than simply affects the department of defence. So far as the defence departments are concerned, in order to be ready for whatever plan may be worked out, we are making a survey of all the positions in which women can be utilized, and are receiving reports from all districts, camps and headquarters as well. One of the branches at headquarters now is the D.A.G.(M)-deputy adjutant general (mobilization). That officer is working with the Department of National War Services, particularly in connection with those activities.
Whatever general work is done with regard to the coordination of women's activities in governmental services will be done by the Department of National War Services, and the defence departments will get their requirements from the Department of National War Services. It is anticipated that each defence service will have its own branch in which women who can be employed will be engaged.

What is the function of the reserve army? As the minister knows, within the last few rveeks their training strength has been cut dowm by at least 50 per

Supply-National Defence
cent, and I believe that those men who joined the reserve army last year did so on the understanding that they would assist their country. But to-day their morale is being definitely destroyed. The minister owes it to the men in the reserve army to tell them what their task is, what is expected of them, and not, merely for the purpose of saving a few dollars, to cut everything from under them at every opportunity.
The commanding officer of my reserve unit has resigned because he was quite dissatisfied with the role that the reserve army has been called upon to play at this time.

As my hon. friend knows, the role of the reserve army has been definitely laid down in instructions from headquarters. One of its primary functions is to provide reinforcements to the active service force, wherever it is a counterpart to a unit in that force. Second, it must be in such a position as to be ready for mobilization should the necessity arise. Third, it must provide aid to the civil power such as has been the function of the reserve army for many years. These are the three outstanding and primary roles.
My hon. friend speaks of camps. He knows the situation in that regard. We have a great many troops; he knows what our plans are *with regard to the movement of troops, and the difficulties in connection with accommodation are considerable. A decision was arrived at with regard to the reserve army, that a certain proportion of its strength should go to camp. The role of the reserve army is well set out. and in a great number of instances reserve units have done remarkably well in the furnishing of reinforcements.
It has been a matter of some disappointment to me in certain instances that the reserve units have not done more. It is said that many men in the reserve army enlisted to do something for their country who did not find it possible to enlist for active service, and at the same time, on top of that, with respect to some units, I have received applications from time to time that units be mobilized. Obviously, one cannot mobilize a unit with any considerable prospect of success if there are not many men in the unit who are prepared to enlist for active service. I do not find fault, but I mention that as one of the difficulties which presented themselves to the department in connection with this very anxious question of reserve units. All of them are eager to serve in some capacity, and many of the communities where they are localized are particularly desirous of being represented in the active service force. But there are difficulties owing to the fact that men who have enlisted with the idea of doing the best they could to 14S73-251
serve their country, in such a capacity as a reserve unit might afford in Canada, have been precluded from taking a more active part for various reasons, business, medical or family.

I wish briefly to bring to the attention of the minister and the government the question of medical services in connection with our armed forces. Let me say at the outset that I am not critical of the personnel which goes to make up those particular forces. It is true that there are many square pegs in round holes in this branch of the force, as perhaps has been said of some other branches. By that I mean that it has been necessary to give special training to certain men in the army medical corps where men could have been found who had had that training in their professional and civilian life. I would say to the minister that the medical profession are not convinced that, having in view efficiency and economy, we have the best set-up at the present time. We have three forces: one for the air, one for the navy and one for the land. It is the general opinion that we have more duplication than is necessary. For instance, in the city of Halifax we have hospitals for the men of the navy, the men of the air force and the men of the army. That is an unnecessary duplication of both buildings and personnel and certainly must cost considerably more money. After all, when men in any of these forces become casualties or become ill, when they reach a hospital they are all in the same category. When you have to set up three distinct arms of medical men, you can well imagine that what appears in the papers is true, that there is a shortage of doctors.
Not if they were all busy.

But they are duplicating work. I am going to suggest how there will not be that shortage if use is made of those who are already in the service. Let me first suggest that instead of spending a good deal of public money for military hospitals, we first make use of the civilian facilities which are already built and equipped and available. That has been done to some extent but not to the extent to which it should be done.
Then, looking further ahead to conditions in the post-war period, if the money were spent on additions to civilian institutions, those could be used to advantage in the after-war period. That is preferable to erecting temporary buildings which will be done away with when the war is over. We could also make use of the staff of these civilian institutions instead of having the military medical staff look after the treatment of men in hospital.

I am also led to believe that there is great duplication in the purchasing of supplies. Old regulations that are in some of the army books are carried out. I have been told by pharmaceutical houses that they receive requisitions for drugs, instruments and other things that are entirely out of date and are not being used in this country.
I bring these suggestions to the ministry not with a view of being critical of the administration. As I say, I have no criticism of the personnel of the army medical corps of the different forces. But I do believe that they could be used to better advantage and that the duplication of services is unnecessary. So far as erecting new hospitals is concerned, that should not be done until such time as civilian institutions are in full use, and when it becomes necessary to build, it should be done as an addition to already existing civilian institutions which are established, and which can be made use of in the post-war period.

As to duplication of
medical services, as my hon. friend knows, the medical service for the air force was separated from that for the army some six or eight or ten months ago after a pretty thorough examination by a medical man who came out from England. I think the ground was that the air force requires special examination on account of the higher medical specifications which are required, and that it was to the advantage of the service that there be separation. My hon. friend will know far better than I the soundness of that view.
The question of the use of civilian hospital facilities has been before us within the last four weeks, and we have found it impossible to lay down any absolute rule that in every case civilian facilities should be used. But we have a rule, and it is being adhered to, that whenever civilian facilities offer themselves the case will be considered on its merits. There is going to be no rigid rule that the army must have a separate hospital no matter what the possibilities are in the particular community where the facilities are needed.
With regard to duplication in purchasing of supplies, I had not heard of that before. My hon. friend also suggested that supplies are being purchased that are outmoded-

And duplication of both
supplies and equipment.
Of course my hon. friend knows that supplies are always bought through the Department of Munitions and Supply. But I will make a note of my hon. friend's point.

I do not know whether the recruiting campaign is entirely to the minister's satisfaction or not. I am not going to argue one way or the other, but it does seem to me that amidst the glamour and excitement of the victoiy loan campaign the mere recruit must feel like the forgotten man. After all, the problem that faces the common man in Canada at the present time is not so simple as it is in England. In England the people do not have to be told that they must fight or die, kill or be killed. The problem here for the majority of people, not perhaps for members of parliament, but for the masses of the people throughout the country, is not so simple as that. Nor is it made simpler by those who keep on reminding us of the inevitable unemployment, poverty and bankruptcy that must follow victory in this war. Those who are responsible for the recruiting campaign could do no more useful work than to make it clear to the Canadian people that the government will no more tolerate losing the peace than they will tolerate losing the war.

There was an announcement in the press a couple of weeks ago that the number of men called for compulsory training for June had been reduced to about 2,700 men. It was our understanding before Easter that there would be some 5,000 men called up every month. Apparently that number has now been reduced. Will the minister explain why that is, and tell us how many there will be in the future?

There is accommodation
for about 40,000 altogether; that is, about
10,000	a month. The basic centres are combined; the active and the reserve recruits are combined in the basic training centres. The more active enlistments there are, the fewer recruits will be necessary. That has been made plain right along; forty thousand is what we are turning out every four months. The more active recruits there are the fewer will have to be called up under the compulsory' training plan.

How many is it expected
there will be during the rest of the summer?
I cannot tell. It depends on the number of active recruits who are enlisted. Does my hon. friend understand that?

Is the minister yet in a
position to make any statement with regard to the escape of the twenty-five or twenty-six German prisoners from the prison camp in northern Ontario?

As my hon. friend knows, a court of inquiry was held under Mr. Justice Embury. The finding of that court was filed

Supply-National Defence
with the department, and the matter is now in the hands of the adjutant general. As a matter of fact, further proceedings are now pending in connection with the matter. I am not in a position to make any statement in regard to it until those proceedings are concluded.

I have not yet asked a question in connection with this department, but there is one thing I should like to know. A short time ago I received a complaint with regard to the central mechanization depot in the city of London. I understand that this is practically an ordinary civilian set-up, except for the fact that it is under the Department of National Defence.
That is a pretty important exception.

At least the employees
there were on a civilian basis; I will put it that way. Unionization of the men was going on; organization was being carried out, and a conciliation board was applied for. In the midst of the discussion the men were notified by a conciliation officer, I believe named Mr. Chapel-
There is no such conciliation officer in my department.

My information as to the name may not be correct, but the men were notified that the government was about to place this depot definitely under the Department of National Defence, and that in these circumstances a collective bargaining agreement could not be negotiated. I should like to know whether the facts were as I have stated them, and whether this depot comes under the Department of National Defence or under the Department of Labour. Both departments seem to be involved in the situation. Could the minister tell me anything about the matter, as far as his department is concerned?

So far as my department is concerned the central mechanization depot at London is under the master general of the ordnance, and is a Department of National Defence organization. The depot was established for the purpose of receiving, storing and issuing mechanically propelled vehicles. It also performs the same function for the spare parts and accessories required to maintain and equip such vehicles. Its purpose includes the performance of any work which may be required upon vehicles between receipt from contractors and issue to military formations, such as the addition of special equipment not included in the main vehicle contract. It will also serve as a central repair depot. There is capacity for storing 14873-251}
3,300 vehicles under cover, and these storage facilities permit the following advantageous practices: (a) the flow of production by the automotive industry may be kept relatively even and therefore at the maximum of efficiency; (b) the full establishment of vehicles for a military formation may be purchased, but any quantity not required during the period prior to active service may be held in reserve; (c) a reserve for unknown emergencies may be held.
Who are employed at this plant? Are they civilian employees?
I think they are ordnance men. I am advised that the depot is in process of 'being turned completely into an ordnance organization.

That is just the point. Up to the present time, according to my information, a large number of civilians have been employed in this work, and it was not until the men became dissatisfied with the rates of pay, which are very considerably lower than those in automobile plants such as General Motors and others, and began to organize, that action was taken to place the men directly under the control of the master general of 'the ordnance, or to militarize the plant. Many of these men, of course, will lose their jobs because of this action, which it is felt was taken to prevent the organization of the men in this plant. That is rather a serious statement for the men involved to make, but it came to me through one of the legitimate trade unions, if I may use that term, and the union officials were very disturbed and wondered if this was going to be a precedent to prevent the organization of men in government plants of this description.

I can only say to my hon. friend that it may have been concurrent with, or synchronized with, or at the same time as, what my hon. friend mentions, but as I understand it the master general of the ordnance intended this to be a military establishment. I will tell my hon. friend the reason for that, as it was given to me. That wa3 the intention in order to give these men training in handling and repairing these vehicles. As the country knows, one of our most difficult jobs is the training of tradesmen and familiarizing them with these vehicles. This was one of the preliminary steps taken to provide, in effect, a trade school where repairs could be made and familiarity acquired with the various vehicles being used. I cannot tell my hon. friend more 'than that.

So that it was intended, some time before this, that this depot would be militarized?
Supply-National Defence

That is my understanding. This matter was not discussed with me at all, but if I had had anything to do with it there would have been no question about it, and I believe the master general of the ordnance had this fully in mind from the very beginning.

Under present regulations, as pointed out by the hon. member for Lake Centre, a man joining the army to-day who has more than two children is obliged to leave a certain number of his children without a subsistence allowance. Is there any intention on the part of the government to change the regulations in this regard? I know men in the unit of which the minister is honorary colonel who have left six children at home, which means that the wife, with an allowance for two children, is required to care for four in addition without provision being made for their maintenance. Is there any intention to change that regulation?

All these matters are
constantly under consideration, but I cannot give my hon. friend any assurance that there is any intention of changing the regulation. I may say that I have made a note of no less than ten different reasons which have been given in this chamber this afternoon as to why men should not enlist. All these matters are being given attention. I can assure hon. members that the recruiting committee. which is in charge of this campaign, have had most of these matters in mind. Notwithstanding all these reasons, however, some of which may be sound and some unsound, I do ask hon. members, though they have given expression to these views here, to do as an old medical officer of mine often suggested: "Don't tell me the difficulties; tell me how to get over them." I ask my hon. friends to do the same thing in connection with this recruiting campaign, because I do not think many of these difficulties are really serious as long as a man is imbued with the spirit mentioned a while ago, the desire to serve his country. I do not wish any hon. member to understand for a moment, however, that because I have not replied to all these matters they have not been considered and are not being kept in mind. Naturally I want to do all I can, and the department wants to do all it can, to make recruiting and army life as attractive as possible under the circumstances, and having regard to the needs and duties which have to be performed.
To supplement my answer to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. perhaps I did not emphasize as I should the fact that the
[Mr Coldwell.]
mechanization depot is a place where vehicles actually owned by the army are kept, and from which they are issued.

I did not know very much about the depot; I just had the complaint. There is one other point to which I think the minister should give his attention, namely, the position of mothers whose sons have enlisted, such sons or mothers having been on relief before the boys joined. The ruling was-I do not know whether it is still in effect-that because the boy was not a wage-earner and in support of his mother before joining up, the mother was not eligible for any allowance. I do not know whether that has been changed, but if it has not, I believe the minister should give it his attention.

I believe the ruling was
changed about nine months ago.

I believe I can say
from experience that it is a mistake for the government to accept in the army men who have big families. Consideration should be given to seeing that they are not recruited in the future.

I should like to know what the agreement is between the dominion government and the Bell Telephone company, through the Department of Public Works, with regard to service to government telephones. I ask the question for several reasons, one of which is that the Bell Telephone company is of course a very powerful organization, charging, in comparison with what we pay in western Canada to provincial telephone companies, a very high rate on short-distance calls. At times there is a difficulty in having calls put through quickly from this building to Toronto and Montreal. I have heard complaints in that regard. Upon making inquiry I have been told the reason is that although the company is making very high profits for the United States parent company, as well as for itself, it has not the necessary trunk lines to give that service to which at least the government of Canada and these buildings ought to be entitled. What is the contract with the Bell Telephone company? What are the rates, and cannot some pressure be brought to bear upon this company, whose profits since the beginning of the war have shown an increase, to give at least this city and this building better telephone connection in return for the very high rates everyone has to pay?

Mr. Chairman, there is a
matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. A building was recently erected at the Lancaster military hospital, at West Saint John, New Brunswick, to be used, I understand, as an isolation hospital or a hospital for contagious diseases. The specifications for the building required the hinges or butts as they are called in the trade, on the inside doors to be of solid bronze. I am informed that these bronze hinges cost about. $6 a pair and that they serve no better purpose and cannot be distinguished from steel chromium-plated hinges, which cost about $1.10 a pair. I should like to know why bronze hinges were used when they cost so much more than the steel chromium-plated hinges. It seems to me that this is a waste
Supply-Public Works

of money and that there is inefficiency on the part of the department in specifying hinges of this kind. I would also point out to the minister that it affords an opportunity for a contractor, if he wants to be unscrupulous, to use steel chromium-plated hinges instead of the bronze hinges called for, because it is impossible to distinguish one from the other.
I would also point out that the specifications provided for steel knobs with cylinder lock on the outside door. This form of knob will rust on exposure to the weather. The specifications should have provided for bronze knobs, which will stand exposure to the weather. I do not know if the minister is in a position to give an explanation now', but it is a matter which I think should be investigated.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for bringing the matter to my attention. I am reminded by the officer here that this building is being erected for the Department of Pensions and National Health and that the specifications had to agree with their requirements. I am not in a position to explain why such a fitting was specified or to give the reason justifying such a requirement, if in reality this fitting was called for by the specifications. In the main I am free to say that I agree with the observations of my hon. friend, but of course there may be some reason which cannot be given at the moment. I will undertake to look into the matter and inform my hon. friend.

I wish to ask the minister a question about the stationary engineers employed by the Department of Public Works in Ottawa. It has been brought to my attention that a number of the stationary engineers employed by the public works department in this city are not receiving the one day rest in seven. If that is so, it is a matter of long standing. I would point out that the Lord's Day Act compels the citizens of Canada to observe a weekly day of rest, and if the situation is as I am told it is, the public works department ought not to be breaking one of Canada's own statutes.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to try the patience of the committee, but while we are on the railway estimates I desire to inform the house that on March 28 last I handed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Cardin) a brief on the subject of the Baie des Chaleurs railway. In substance, this brief stated:
Work has been begun on the establishment of a naval base and an air base at Gaspe. Now that the battle of the Atlantic is under way and that German submarines and cruisers are only some three hundred miles from our eastern coasts, this project is of incommensurable importance. It is quite possible that the enemy may enter the gulf of St. Lawrence and attack the Gaspe coast, which lies open and defenceless. Thus the urgent need of pushing forward the organization of these two defence bases.
In order to establish communication with these bases, to move the requisite supplies, material and troops, it is a matter of imperative necessity and immediate urgency to improve the Baie des Chaleurs railway. This line, some two hundred miles in length, is the property of the Canadian National Railways. At present, it cannot carry heavy locomotives and freight cars cannot be loaded to full capacity on account of the poor condition of the line. The road-bed needs to be ballasted throughout its entire length and light rails replaced by heavy ones over a length of 45 miles. This would ensure a twofold result- the normal defence of the Gaspe peninsula and the whole country in wartime, and normal railway facilities in time of peace.
May I point out further that while industrial activity, employment and prosperity are the rule in most sections of the country at present, the Gaspe peninsula remains in a state of unemployment and comparative poverty. Doubtless it would be difficult to establish war industries in that section of the country. But that could be made up for by improving the railway line. The result would be (a) to provide work for the unemployed; (b) to strengthen our national defence; (c) to anticipate postwar needs, and (d) to give justice to this section of the country which has never enjoyed its share in the Canadian confederation and has always been looked upon as a poor relation.
This is not the first time that the house lias heard of the Gaspe railroad. My predecessor, Hon. Charles Marcil, frequently pointed out the poor condition of the line
t'Mr. Cardin.]
and the state of inferiority in which the Gaspe people found themselves as a result.
Many of the older members will recall the fine personality of Hon. Charles Marcil. An intimate friend and counsellor of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, he represented Bonaventure during thirty-seven years without interruption and without suffering defeat at the polls. A most eloquent speaker, he often held the house spellbound. He was rightly called golden-tongued. He had the honour of accompanying Sir Wilfrid Laurier from one end of the country to the other during the campaigns of 1904, 1908 and 1911.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, my predecessor, Mr. Marcil frequently called the house's attention to the Gaspe railroad. I shall quote from a speech he delivered from this floor on the 21st of June, 1923, as the words he uttered then are applicable to the present situation:
The two counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure are inhabited by 60,000 people, and we could easily have three times that population if we had a proper railway service. These two constituencies cover 10,000 square miles of the most fertile territory in the province of Quebec, with a double advantage of being situated by the sea, having thousands of miles of timber and pulpwood, mineral resources, fertile soil, and splendid fisheries producing some of the finest fish of the North American continent. Our rivers are visited yearly by the cream of American and Canadian society. Nevertheless the district has remained in a quiescent state. During the decade from 1911 to 1921, the population increased by only 500. Why? Because the industries in both Gaspe and Bonaventure, one after another moved away across the Baie des Chaleurs to the Intercolonial where they could get service over which they could send their produce. At Nouvelle, to begin with, the Province of Quebec Lumber Association transferred all its lumber over to Dalhousie, and it is operating on the main line of the Intercolonial. The same thing happened at Bonaventure and New Richmond where the mills of the McLean Lumber Corporation were transferred to Bathurst, and to-day we witness the spectacle of this lumber being cut in these two counties and being transported in booms across the Baie des Chaleurs, a distance ranging from 25 to 50 miles, to be sawn and placed on board cars to be exported to the Canadian and American markets at great disadvantage and loss. The result of this is that the young people are leaving these two counties daily, and settling, unfortunately a large number of them, in the United States. We are losing our population, and this because we have not an efficient railway service which would develop the resources of these constituencies as they should be developed.
Hon. Mr. Marcil's speeches always ended with a request to the government of the day to have the Baie des Chaleurs railroad made part of the Canadian National Railways.
Finally in 1928, thanks to the personal intervention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. JUNE 13, 1941	3981

Lapointe), the Baie des Chaleurs road was taken over by the Liberal government and incorporated into the national system.
I wish here to convey to the Minister of Justice the gratitude of the Gaspe people for this act of justice. In spite of the minister's well-known modesty, we have been definitely apprised of the fact that he is responsible for the success met by Hon. Mr. Marcil in attaining the object of his oft-repeated requests. The Minister of Justice has earned the admiration and gratefulness of the people of Gaspe for having thrown all the weight of his influence on the side of their section of the country.
As a consequence, Mr. Chairman, the Baie des Chaleurs railway has been operated by the Canadian National railways for almost thirteen years. Many complaints have been attended to; we enjoy freight rates that are considerably lower than formerly; the right of way is better kept and the service much more convenient than under the old management.
However, I must say, as suggested in the brief from which I quoted that we are still a long way from perfection. The Canadian National boasts of having expended $1,300,000 in the last twelve years in improvements of all sorts. Well, Mr. Chairman, this line was in such a bad way, that even the expenditure of this seemingly large sum of money still leaves it in a deplorable state.
Two hundred miles of that line require ballasting. In many places it follows the shore so closely that protection walls had to be built to check the eroding effect of the sea. Many of those works are in such a bad shape that people are fearful, and not without cause, when travelling over these precipices.

Furthermore, and I presume to call the Minister of Transport's attention to this fact, all through the spring period the trains had to reduce their speed to ten or twenty miles an hour on account of the poor condition of the right of way. At the moment, of

Ships have to be assembled somewhere in large numbers in order that warships may escort them across the sea, and some other ports in Canada are suffering in consequence of that assembly. to doing, and if the war is prolonged and becomes intensified there is still a possibility that this route may be of immense value to Canada and Great Britain. It is short; it is well north, and it would save a perilous passage for ships along the Atlantic coast. I do not profess to know much about shipping or naval affairs; but if the war is prolonged, the conservatism of the authorities may be broken down, and this route may yet be a valuable outlet for supplies to Great Britain. I am glad to know that the road and the facilities are being maintained, and even if we are spending a great deal of money this year and taking a serious deficit, I believe it is worth while keeping everything in good shape, because the time may come in this war when we shall find that route a useful one.

I should like to say a word or two on this question because, as it happens, the port of Churchill is in my constituency. The fact of the matter is that Churchill has suffered in the last five or six years from conditions beyond the control of any government. In 1937-38 no grain was shipped there. Why? Because in that year Saskatchewan did not produce enough wheat to meet its own requirements. From the date of the opening of the port there has been a steady increase in business until adverse conditions arose.
What the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggested a moment ago was correct. There was a conservatism in shipping circles regarding the practicability of the Hudson bay route, but from the first or second year of its use as a port the insurance rates on cargoes of grain and on hulls were reduced, not to the point they 'would ultimately reach but considerably.
The hon. member for Lethbridge offers criticism because the port has not been used in the last two years. Well, shipping in Great Britain since the outbreak of war has been under the direction of the minister of shipping, and they will not send ships to Churchill on account of the risk involved. The ship would come out through the Hudson bay strait, but submarines are operating not very far off the coast of Greenland, a very short distance indeed from the outlet of the strait, and consequently cargo vessels are exposed to the risk of sinking by submarines unless accompanied by convoy. Therefore this route is not practicable at the moment.
I am as much interested as any hon. member in seeing the port developed. I have been one of its consistent advocates from the earliest date, and I am as much convinced as the member for Rosetown-Biggar that the day will come, not perhaps in the next few years but some time, when the route

will be one of the great trade routes of the world. There are no doubt practical difficulties to-day against it, but not from lack of sympathy on the part of the Minister of Transport or of the government. The people in the district fully recognize the difficulties. When the war is over, however, and we return to peaceful conditions and safety at sea, the port will come into its own and will be used.
It is worth while mentioning that there is less than one hundred miles difference in distance as between that port and the port of Montreal in relation to Liverpool, and consequently all that area which lies in the northwestern and central part of Saskatchewan is many hundreds of miles closer to Liverpool by that route than by Montreal or Vancouver. Churchill is not the only port that has suffered from war conditions. Let the hon. member inquire as to the amount of wheat that has gone out of Vancouver in the last eighteen months, and he will find it' has been practically stationary so far as shipments to Great Britain are concerned.
These are conditions that arise out of the war and they are beyond the control of the Minister of Transport. They are beyond the control of the government, and they will not be remedied until the war is over; but I have every confidence in the future of the port when the war is over and we return to peaceful conditions.

Personally, I think this committee should be seriously concerned with what has happened to the broadcasting corporation.
First, it is a public utility, owned by the people of Canada, and, as is necessary in all such cases, it is essential that this house be eternally vigilant. There are private interests in the picture which would like to displace it and undertake the work themselves. The present development in the corporation gives rise to very grave concern to many of us who have believed for a number of years in publicly owned radio. We have

When the present general manager, Major Murray, was appointed, the appointment was generally approved on account of his long association with the British Broadcasting Corporation and with publicly owned radio. Whatever may have been the importance of radio in peace time, during the war it becomes of primary significance from the point of view of the country's war effort. We cannot fail to realize the use which the totalitarian powers have made of radio as a system of propaganda for their cause. I am not protesting, because I believe the members of the government should be given every facility to address the people of Canada in war time; but it is also wise, it seems to me, to prevent any idea that the government has a monopoly of radio broadcasting. Since that return was tabled, three broadcasts, which were described when the speakers were introduced as "experimental broadcasts", have been made, by the leader of the opposition, the leader of the social credit group, and myself.
I wish now to deal with some of the disclosures which were made in the parliamentary return tabled on May 16 in answer to certain questions which I had addressed to the minister.
According to that return, the by-laws of the corporation have been amended lately in such a way as to alter fundamentally the whole structure of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation constitution, and to alter it for the worse. In effect, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will now have three managers-the general manager, the assistant general manager, and the executive committee of the board. This is contrary to the clear recommendations of the 1936 parliamentary committee, and contrary also to the clear intention of the act. The report of the committee stated, at page 784, as recommendation No. 1:
1.	It has been amply demonstrated that a commission of three cannot be moulded into a unit that can formulate and execute policy

successfully. Evidence adduced before this committee has made it apparent that under the existing organization there has been a lack of coordination in dealing with some major questions.
It goes on to say:
1(a). After carefully reviewing the administration of radio broadcasting, we have reached the conclusion that the recommendation of the 1934 committee, namely "that in the opinion of your committee radio broadcasting can best be conducted by a general manager", is justified in all respects, and your committee hereby endorses and repeats that recommendation.
The act provides, in section 6:
There shall be a general manager who shall be chief executive of the corporation.
This policy of unified management and control was carefully embodied in a former by-law of the corporation, in which the general manager is made the chief executive officer, subject only to the direction of the board of governors. The assistant manager is made responsible to him, as is every other department, and he alone is given the power of employment, dismissal, and remuneration of employees, with the exception of anyone receiving more than $4,000 a year.
All this was done as a result of the 1936 parliamentary committee report and was fully approved by the 1938 and 1939 parliamentary committees. The following quotation from the 1938 committee report is relevant:
Your committee believes that the constitution of the corporation ensuring a proper division between policy and management and a degree of flexibility and independence essential to the medium of broadcasting, together with ultimate parliamentary control, is well suited to the purpose for which it was created.
Furthermore, this point was emphasized above all others in the report of Mr. J. C. Thompson, which was tabled in this house some time ago. The whole plan of administration which he recommends throughout his report, and which he illustrates in appendix F attached to that report, hinges upon his opinion that efficient management requires "unified control of operations throughout Canada."
In short, four parliamentary committees, four statements by the heads of the corporation, and this latest survey by Mr. Thompson, all agree that to divide the management, to divide control and responsibility in an organization like the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, is to court disaster. In fact, as the 1936 report stated, it was precisely such divided authority which caused the difficulty under the former broadcasting commission and which brought about the changes that were recommended in that year. Yet the board of governors, and the government by the passage of order in council P.C. 2845, have seen fit to
ignore all this evidence, and the recommendations of these committees and the act itself, and to reintroduce precisely the very arrangements which experience had proven to be disastrous.
Who is in charge of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation now? According to the return, the following is the confusing and confused situation. The general manager is in charge of certain departments. The assistant general manager is in charge of certain other departments. The former has the right of employing staff for certain of the departments, while the latter-

Major Murray has to be responsible "for the carrying out of the provisions of the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936, and of the by-laws and regulations made thereunder," while Doctor Frigon is to be responsible "for the internal management of the affairs of the corporation." To add to this confusion, neither of these gentlemen is to be responsible to the other, but both are to be subject to management and control by the executive committee, which apparently is to have the final say.
Note that another thing which wrecked the old radio commission was that, in fields of policy and management, there was no clearly defined line of separation; and that, of course, is something which is essential to the organization of any efficient body such as the broadcasting corporation.
The radio act sought to achieve this essential condition by putting management in the hands of the manager and leaving policy to the board. But the new by-laws upset all this. Members of the board who form the executive committee are given the final managerial authority -men who were not appointed for that purpose, nor with those particular qualifications for that particular function in mind. Can anyone in this house think of a more inefficient and a worse form of divided management?
Why was all this considered necessary? The minister last autumn certainly implied, and gave the house the impression by his silence, that he was satisfied with the corporation's management. Indeed, the board of governors went further. They passed a resolution which was published in the press on November 27, 1940, proclaiming "their full and complete confidence in the general manager." Yet, I submit, a clearer case of none too gentle demotion cannot be found. One cannot escape

I now come to a question to which this committee should demand a very clear answer: To whom is the corporation responsible, and what is its status? Ever since its formation in 1936, the government and the minister have maintained that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was an independent body similar in status to the Canadian National Railways. On this ground, information regarding the internal management of the corporation was refused in this house on several occasions. For this reason, too, there were parliamentary committees in 1938 and 1939 to inquire into the affairs of the corporation. To the latter, Mr. L. W. Brockington, chairman of the board of governors, made an exhaustive statement

on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, during which he had the following to say on the point of the corporation's status:
I make this submission as our view of our own position. We are not .part of the government of Canada. We are not civil servants, nor part of the civil service. . . . We are trustees for the payers of licences. In other words, we are trustees for that class in the community which can be described as licensed listeners. They include people who speak the French language and people who speak the English language; they include Liberals, Conservatives, Social Crediters, members of the C.C.F. party and members indeed of many other organizations, both those which are in esse and in posse. Our listeners represent the east and the west, the rich and the poor, and for them we are trustees.
Later in his presentation, Mr. Brockington gives the reasons why the 1936 parliamentary committee recommended that the corporation be set up, as it was, as a separate corporation under a radio act. He said that this was necessary in the case of broadcasting, and I quote again:
(a)	because, from all points of view, it is in fact in the nature of a business;
(b)	because the character of broadcasting requires the utmost flexibility of administration;
(c)	because the national broadcasting authority must be removed from the direct control of the government of the day and be nonpartisan and independent.
Many references could be given to statements by the Prime Minister, and by the Minister of Munitions and Supply while he was Minister of Transport, stressing that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was an autonomous corporation. I shall give one or two. In a letter written on behalf of the Prime Minister on November 21, 1939, to the Ontario secretary of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, the following paragraph occurs:
Mr. King wishes me to point out that the relationship between the government and the corporation had not been altered by the existence of a state of war, except that the censorship regulations apply to broadcasting as to other forms of publicity. The board of governors of the corporation have retained full control of broadcasting, and of the arrangement of programmes, in accordance with the responsibility imposed upon them by parliament.
Then the Minister of Munitions and Supply made the following statement in this house on January 20, 1939, as reported at page 192 of Hansard:
I might remind hon. gentlemen that the Canadian broadcasting corporation is an autonomous body, set up by this parliament under the broadcasting act of 1936, which superseded the broadcasting act of 1932 sponsored by hon. gentlemen opposite. Surely the Prime Minister, and perhaps the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who has been exceedingly busy, have not fully realized what has been happening. If they do realize it, and allow this condition to continue, they and the entire government are guilty of seriously damaging proper democratic and parliamentary control of a public utility which is of great importance to this country for the successful prosecution of the war and the maintenance of national unity.
I think I have said enough to substantiate my former statements that conditions in the broadcasting corporation are serious. I suggest that the recent actions of the government and the board show clearly that they have been aware of the seriousness of the situation.
Why then was a parliamentary committee not appointed when there was a request for it in the house and in many sections of the press? Representatives of the leading private broadcasting interests appeared before the board of governors to demand the right to increase their power to the limits allowed under the Havana agreement.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my purpose at this stage of the session to make any extended remarks in reply to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. It seems to me, however, that the hon. gentleman is exceedingly inconsistent in his argument, in that in one breath he argues that this corporation is a department of the government, and, in the next, that it is an independent corporation.
May I suggest that this is exactly what the minister has been doing, and I was trying to find out exactly what it was.

This is my interpretation. This is a corporation set up by an act of parliament. The members of the corporation are the governors. The powers of the board of governors are the powers granted to them by an act of parliament, and the management of the corporation is vested in that board. Neither the minister in charge of the department nor any parliamentary committee has authority to manage the corporation. A parliamentary committee can recommend to the government any change in the broadcasting act. The government can appoint the governors of the corporation. The minister in charge of the department is the channel of communication between the board of governors and parliament and between the board of governors and the governor in council; but the management of the broadcasting corporation has been vested by this parliament in the board of governors. During the time I was in charge of the department, after the last broadcasting act was passed by this house, I was the channel of communication between the board of governors and this parliament and between the board and the government of Canada; but I was always careful to respect the position that it was the board of governors who were operating the corporation.
As to the position of the employees of the broadcasting corporation, that is entirely a legal matter; and in legal matters we of the government rely upon the Department of Justice, as we are bound to do. The question of whether the employees of the corporation are in the position of being employees of an independent corporation, or whether they are, in fact, employees of an emanation of the crown, is a legal question, depending entirely upon the position in which they were placed by the act of this parliament establishing the corporation. The Department of Justice has

considered the matter and has handed down a ruling that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is an emanation of the crown, and that the employees are in fact employees of the crown. As I say, that is a legal decision, and I do not think it is for me or for any other member of parliament to argue with the Department of Justice as to the correctness of that decision.
My hon. friend stated that changes have been made which have destroyed the position of the corporation. Those changes were very minor indeed. One change was that a new officer has been appointed, in the person of a comptroller. As companies grow and staff matters become more complex, it is quite customary to appoint a comptroller; that is, a man especially entrusted with the internal audit of expenditures and the control of staff. The changes in the by-laws had to do with the appointment of the comptroller, and the duties of that office were added to those of the assistant general manager. At the same time the control was strengthened somewhat to some extent by the appointment of an executive committee which could meet more frequently than the board as a whole, and which was given additional responsibilities particularly in connection with the financial control of the corporation.
I might point out that during the last year the corporation has been under some stress and strain due to the fact that a number of its senior officers have had to spend long periods of time in the British isles helping out the corporation during a difficult period there. As a result, the other senior officers of the corporation were called upon to double up in their duties, and a certain laxity of financial control was called to my attention by the auditor general. I reported the communication of the auditor general, who is also the auditor of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to the board of directors, and asked them to take prompt steps. The steps taken were those which the board of directors thought necessary to overcome the lack of financial control which had been apparent, as a result of the auditor general's report.
The situation referred to by the auditor general was a very small matter in dollars and cents, and, when called to the attention of the board, was immediately corrected. Obviously, however, it was the duty of the board to take steps to see that the controls were tightened so that a similar situation could not arise again. I make no apologies for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or its management. I believe it is a stronger institution to-day than it has been in any time in its history. Here is question 10 which was asked by the the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and answered on May 16:

The answer to that was:

My hon. friend's twelfth question was:

The answer to that was:
