These amounts, of course, were in addition to the salary of S13,600 paid to the general manager and $12,000 paid to the assistant general manager.
Here is the letter of the auditor general to the minister, dated February 25:
Dear Mr. Howe:
The broadcasting act places at the command of the broadcasting corporation certain moneys and, within the terms of the act, the corporation decides on the purposes to which these moneys are to be put.
Section 19 gives to you, as minister, powers with respect to the accounting system, reports, et cetera, and the following section names this office as auditor of the corporation.
Certain points have been brought to my notice, and being in doubt as to the authority to whose notice I should bring them, I address this letter to you.
The act provides that the general manager is to be appointed by the governor in council. This was done and the salary named by order in council. On examining the records of the corporation, it is observed that an allowance at the date of $4,800 "at the base of operations", was authorized by the board, "pending an adjustment in the general manager's salary, as requested by the board." In view of the language used, the question arises as to the administrative power to give such a direction, if the true interpretation to be given to the act is that payments to the general manager are within the sole discretion of the governor in council.
Associated with this is a second point which arises out of the fact that last spring the Minister of Finance gave to the House of Commons an explanation of the interpretation to be given by the income tax authorities to
living allowances paid to various men on war work for the crown. The corporation has left to the general manager the question of deciding what officers may be paid per diem allowances and the amounts which may be claimed, in lieu of actual details, when away from their official stations on official business. The accounts show that $20 is the amount claimed by the general manager, but this has apparently been selected by himself as being commensurate with his disbursements. The sum involved is not of concern, but it seems to me probable that the decision in such a matter is associated with the powers of the governor in council, or is one which rests on the board.
After you have had an opportunity to peruse the attached memorandum-which was prepared on my instructions to illustrate the problem- might I be informed:
(a)	If you are satisfied that the corporation acted within its powers in granting the $4,800 annual allowance to the general manager? and
(b)	If the establishing of a per diem travel allowance to the general manager is a subject of concern to the governor in council?
Yours faithfully,
Watson Sellar,
Auditor General.
I think the committee is entitled to a full statement as to the answers which the minister made to the auditor general. If an allowance of $4,800 has been provided, why this additional amount of $5,697.90 "to cover expenses incurred while absent from base of operations?"

The legal position is this. Under the broadcasting act the salaries of the general manager and assistant general manager are fixed by order in council. Early in the history of the broadcasting corporation the board of governors in its judgment granted an allowance to the general manager. I protested at the time, taking the view that the granting of special compensation to the general manager was a function of the governor in council. However, the question was referred to the justice department, and the justice department determined that the board of governors had the right to fix an expense allowance for the manager and the assistant general manager. The right was established several years ago. I replied to the auditor general that the matter of an allowance was one for the board of governors to determine; that it was a matter of internal management, but that the situation called to my attention was a matter of concern to the government and that we had referred his letter to the board of governors and asked them to examine the situation and to take appropriate action.
The action taken by the board of governors is a matter of internal management that is not discussed in this House of Commons. It can be looked into by a parliamentary committee at an appropriate time, but it is not a matter that I can discuss here because I had

no part in the action taken. It was taken by the board of governors in the course of their duties.
I might point out, however, that we have had demands for parliamentary committees on three or four occasions, and we have a demand now. We have had three parliamentary committees on radio since the broadcasting act was passed, and to the best of my knowledge and belief those three parliamentary *committees have not changed the broadcasting act in one iota from the act as it passed in 1936. I have the greatest confidence in the world that if another parliamentary committee on radio were held in 1941 or in 1942, the results would be exactly the same as from the three preceding parliamentary committees.
I do not think it would be a question of changing the act. That is not the point at issue.
That is the only way by which the conduct of the broadcasting corporation can be affected.

As a matter of fact, I think the board of governors has, during the past week or so, departed from the original intention of the parliamentary committee and of the act itself. I was not arguing particularly about the labour situation. I introduced that only incidentally. I have the third and final report of the committee containing the recommendations, dated May 26, 1936. Let me just make this one sentence stand out. I quote from the report:
That in the opinion of your committee radio broadcasting could best be conducted by a general manager.
That was a reiteration of the recommendation of the parliamentary committee of 1934.
But the general manager is in sole charge of broadcasting to-day.
No; he is not.
What does he not do about broadcasting?

I have here the new by-laws of the corporation, adopted April 29, 1941, and I find this:
(3) Subject to the control of the board of governors the executive committee shall have power-
Not the general manager:
(a)	to manage the affairs of the corporation, to control its finances and to supervise its operations, in accordance with the general policies laid down by the board of governors;
(b)	to define the functions, duties and responsibilities of the officers and employees of the corporation and to direct them in the performance of their duties.

One cannot imagine the board of governors not having the powers my hon.

friend suggests. The board of governors are delegating their powers to a smaller number of themselves.

I would say to the minister that they delegate to this executive committee the powers that ought to lie in the general manager, because surely it is the function of the general manager to direct the officers and employees of the corporation.
Yes.

Here we are told that
it is the function of the executive committee. What I am objecting to is that we have gone back to exactly the same position in which the old commission found itself before the Radio Act. If we look into the new bylaws we find the other divided authority:
8. (1) (a) The general manager of the corporation shall be its chief executive officer, and, subject to the direction of the board of governors or of the executive committee, he shall have charge of programmes, of policies, and relations of the corporation with the press and the public and be responsible for the carrying out of the provisions of the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936, and of the by-laws and regulations made thereunder.
(b)	The general manager shall have authority to appoint the officers and other employees of the corporation other than-
Authority over other employees is taken away from him.
-the technical, commercial or business staff, but such appointments and the salary rates of these appointees shall be subject to the approval of the executive committee.
In other words, power which lay with the general manager now rests with the executive committee.
The by-laws state:
He may at any time suspend for cause any such officer or employee.
(c)	He may delegate any of his powers to the assistant general manager, or to any officer or employee of the corporation.
Then we come to the assistant general manager.
8. "(2) (a) The assistant general manager, subject to the direction of the board of governors, or the executive committee-
Note this.
*-shall have charge of the technical and commercial operations of the corporation;
No longer is there a general manager managing the corporation. The assistant general manager is removed from his control entirely; he is to be subject to the direction of the board of governors, or the executive committee, and he

-shall have charge of the technical and commercial operations of the corporation; he shall be responsible for the internal management of the affairs of the corporation, and shall fulfil-
What?

-'the duties which may at any time be delegated to him by the board of governors or by the executive committee and shall exercise the powers of the general manager in his absence.
In other words, the assistant general manager is taken out from under the control of the manager, although the recommendation of the parliamentary committee of 1936 was that "in the opinion of your committee radio broadcasting can best be conducted by a general manager." That conclusion was a reiteration of the recommendations of 1934 and was incorporated in the statute. Then:
(b) The assistant general manager shall have authority to appoint the technical, commercial and business staff of the corporation, but such appointments and the salary rates of such appointees shall be subject to the approval of the executive committee-
Not of the general manager, ever, but of the executive committee.
He may at any time suspend for cause any such officer or employee.
On the other point, we have the position of comptroller which the minister mentioned, and which I think is an excellent move in the right direction. The comptroller shall report direct to the board of governors or to the executive committee. That is quite proper; no one can have any objection to that. In the event of there being no comptroller of finance, or in his absence, the powers shall be exercised by the general manager or the assistant general manager or any officer designated by the board of governors and the executive committee. The financial control, I quite agree, is where it ought to be. But I submit that the purpose at the time of the passing of the broadcasting act, the recommendation of the parliamentary committee in 1934, reiterated in 1934, endorsed in 1938 and 1939, was for a unified management of the corporation, and to-day we have the assistant general manager taken from under the control of the manager, and the executive committee assuming managerial powers which ought not to lie in the committee. That is my contention, not that I was talking about the legal status of the corporation in order to deal with labour disputes, although in that respect, may I add, we cannot have it both ways. If it is a government corporation, an emanation of the crown, then of course this house cannot deal with labour disputes between the corporation and its employees, nor can we ask for and receive reports in this house regarding the corporation. If, on the other hand, it is a corporation like the Canadian National Railways, which I believe it to be, then we have the right to ask for all particulars in the house, and the employees have the right, like the Canadian National Railway employees, to
organize a union and negotiate for conditions with the corporation. But that was not the point I was making.
The point was that there has been a distinct change in the whole set-up of the corporation in the last month or so. To-day we have the executive committee becoming the manager, the general manager demoted, and the assistant manager, with certain duties, reporting not to the general manager but direct to the executive committee. The whole basis of the corporation, as we have known it, has been destroyed.
I do not wish to prolong the discussion. I understood that the Prime Minister said that this organization had been transferred to the Department of National War Services. Is that correct?
Yes.

I should like to take the opportunity of commending the government for this wise move. I believe that that is where the organization should belong. I do not believe that the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who is burdened in many directions, should be burdened with this. I urge upon the newly elected Minister of National War Services that he give careful consideration, to the recommendation made this evening by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, namely, to set up a committee to look into this whole question at the next session of parliament.

10J,. Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. $40,000.

The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), speaking last night on estimates pertaining to labour, took occasion to say something about manufacturers and their unfair treatment of their employees. There are undoubtedly some manufacturers who in the past have not perhaps treated their employees as they should have done, but the statement of the hon. member was all-embracing and included everybody. That is not the situation. There are many earnest and sincere manufacturers and businessmen who do treat their employees as employees should be treated, in a spirit of brotherly love, which enjoins a man to follow the Golden Rule and do unto others as he would have others do unto him. I myself was a member of a trade union some thirty-five years ago, and in those days I was fairly well posted on trade unionism. I have not 
been a member for a long time because I graduated from the plant to the executive section of the business, and in my experience I have had both sides of plant life. My experience in plant life has been that managers who treat their men as they should be treated get much more out of them than do those managers who fail to treat their employees properly. A live manager who wishes to obtain the greatest output does, as he should, treat his men properly, just as he would like to be treated, or as he felt he should be treated when he himself was an employee.
I have found, in the course of many dealings with labour leaders, that they too are anxious to avoid strikes. A real representative of labour, a first-class union man, tries at all times to maintain harmony between men and employers, and at the same time he does his best to get fair play for the men. I have found labour leaders, times without number, doing everything they could to avoid calling out their men. Such leaders should be complimented upon their sincerity. Now is the time, if ever there was such a time, when harmony should be encouraged in every possible way; for to-day all should be united, both men and employers, in a common desire to produce the utmost in order to win the war. That is our main objective. Therefore the department, under this vote for the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, should try, and perhaps it is trying, to bring about harmony.
The minister has had a good deal of experience because he has had much to do in his time with adjusting disputes between men and employers. For years I have known of his activities in such matters, and he should be qualified so to direct his department as to avoid to the last limit any dispute between employers and their men, in view of the necessity of producing for war purposes. I have a high regard for my hon. friends to the left. They are doing their best as they see it to represent labour, but I am and I have been a practical labour man-not lately perhaps, because it is some years since I laboured, although in former years I did labour, and I laboured hard in plants. I know, therefore, what labour conditions should be and what labour men should do. As I say, I was one myself. The labour unions have done a great deal and they deserve credit. I have seen much improvement in plant life through the earnest intentions of labour leaders- honest leaders-working for the betterment of the conditions of their men. On the other hand, I know many employers who have diligently endeavoured to improve the conditions of their working men. It was that way in the plant with which I was associated.

Supply-Labour-Industrial Disputes
Where you have harmony between employers and men, there is much more production. A strike is at all times not only contrary to the welfare of the men themselves but injurious to the plant as well. Therefore every earnest man, be he employer or agent of a union, tries to avoid strikes. Part of the trouble in Toronto at the moment is due to the fact that the government itself now controls certain plants there and, doing as the government should do, it gives good wages and the best working conditions. This has had an effect on a large number of employees in plants owned by private individuals. Whether the plants of private individuals are able to live up to the standards set by the government I do not know, but some of the strikes which have recently occurred in Toronto have come about because the private plants felt unable to maintain standards set by government. Every effort should be made to avoid strikes.
Since the war broke out, many of the plants-not so many lately-have operated three shifts a day. Many have reduced the number to two shifts of ten hours each, and they say that they are getting good results, but other plants still operate three shifts. One man told me last Saturday that a certain plant operates three shifts a day of eight hours each, but the shifts alternate. Using an arbitrary figure, I presume one shift would start at midnight and work until eight in the morning, another from eight until four in the afternoon, and a third from four until midnight, and they vary from hour to hour, so that often one of the shifts will work all night. Those men who have been working all night think there should be a distinction in the wages received as between those working at night and those working in the daytime. There is something in that. There should be some adjustment in favour of those who work at night, and those who work in the daytime would get the benefit of the adjustment when it was their turn to work at night. That is one cause of complaint.
Then I am informed that there is considerable child labour. I know that is supposed to be under the control of the province. In Newr York state they recently adopted a child labour law called the Nunan-Moffat law, which prohibits child labour, and where a plant uses child labour they prohibit the transport of the material produced in that plant over the roads or the transportation services of the state. I see a lot of very young-looking people going to work here; they look less than sixteen to me.
In conclusion, I would just say that we all look to the minister to use the conciliation methods in every possible way between employers and men in order to keep the plants M873-253
going, and see to it that fair play prevails all round, fair play for the company and fair play for the men, because men cannot do a good day's work if they are dissatisfied, and furthermore they are liable to be injured while thinking about their conditions. Therefore every effort should be made to have men happy at their work.
I understand the hon. member for Davenport is an employer of labour.
I was also an employee, but held a responsible position for many years.
I was going to say that it is too bad there are not more employers who have the same attitude of mind as the hon. member with respect to the questions he has just been discussing.
I should have said I was an executive official.

I wish to bring something to the attention of the Minister of Labour. I refer specifically to the Hamilton plant where at the present time the government is in the position of employer. I do so on account of the fact that the Minister of Labour a few days ago, in answer to a question as to the number of strikes in Canada at the present time, answered that there were none of which he knew.
In war industries. That was this morning.

I have received from the
steel workers organizing committee a copy of a resolution which was sent to the Prime Minister, and I presume the Minister of Labour is familiar with the subject matter of it. If conditions in that plant are as set out, then I think the Minister of Labour under his conciliation machinery should take immediate steps to iron out that situation.
I find myself in this position, being a member of a union and this house closing within a few days. I go back to a district where there is considerable unrest, and, as pointed out by the hon. member for Davenport, men who are interested in the legitimate unions do at all times use whatever influence they have in the unions to avoid strikes and live up to collective agreements and so forth. That has always been and will in the future be my attitude. While the house is in session, I believe the great majority of the men who have grievances that might culminate in stoppage of work will be marking time, thinking that this house will enact some legislation which will give them a way out of their difficulties other than a strike or stoppage of

work. But with the attitude that the government apparently have been taking with respect to the implementation of order in council 7440, which is the basis to-day for the settlement of all disputes in labour, if we leave with the decisions that have been rendered and the interpretations that have been placed on that order in council standing as they are without doing something to clarify them, I am afraid that after this house adjourns we may run into an epidemic of trouble. That is why I rise at this time.
I think the minister would be well advised if he studied the subject matter of the resolution to which I have referred, and if the controller in the Hamilton plant at the present time is taking the attitude said to be taken in respect of conciliation, recognition of the union and the extension of his power there to probe the matters that apparently are bothering the men employed in that plant, it w'ould be basis upon which other difficulties across the country might be settled. If the government as employer set the example for the other plants in the country with respect to that order in council and its powers as related to labour disputes, in my opinion that would be doing something to avoid the troubles that I see in the future unless something like that is done.
Another board which, I believe, has reported recently to the minister, is that set up for the purpose of examining into the situation of the railway employees with respect to bonus and so forth, representing, I think, some eighteen different organizations in the railway running trades. I understand that is a split decision; that there is a majority and minority report. The minister is now in this position: if I understand order in council 7440 correctly, if a conciliation board render a decision and have erred in their judgment, the Minister of Labour has the power to review that position, and if it is not in accordance with his interpretation of the order in council, or if the intention of the order has not been carried out, he can reinstruct that board and see that a proper decision is given.
If that were done, I think much of the trouble we have been running into would be avoided. I see most of the men who sit on these boards. I read and interpret that order in council as I think it was intended to be interpreted and see no difficulty with respect to its administration. There is much latitude given; the language is very clear, and I think anyone who misunderstands it does so deliberately, working in the interest of someone else. In the final analysis, however, the Minister of Labour has the right to interpret it.

In connection with that railway matter no decision has yet been made public. I should like the Minister of Labour to give an interpretation now of how he thinks order in council 7440 should apply to that case, and to state what he is prepared to do with respect to eliminating the difficulty that exists in that Hamilton plant at the present time.

In connection with the Hamilton plant, as the hon. member is aware a board has been set up there. The board is reconvening on Monday. I am given to understand that there are certain things to be ironed out in that plant. I do not wish to anticipate what the board will do. It would not be fair to them, but I believe that when they meet on Monday, a genuine effort will be made to iron out the difficulties.
In connection with the railway matter, that report was received last night. I have not yet had an opportunity to review it; but, as the hon. member correctly points out, the right of review is specifically provided, and I can assure him that the report will be reviewed very carefully.

As outlined in the annual report, some years ago the federal government, in cooperation with the provinces and municipalities, entered into a resettlement plan under which settlers in a number of provinces were reestablished on the land. Last year I brought before the house some of the conditions that prevailed in the districts where these new settlers were living. Some hon. members came to the conclusion that I was referring to all the farmers of Saskatchewan as living under those conditions, which, of course, was not my contention at all. I was confining my remarks to the conditions that prevailed in those areas in which the people were being reestablished under these government schemes.
I think this government has followed a mistaken policy in discontinuing assistance towards this important work at this time. The other

night I raised the question when the agriculture estimates were before the committee, and the Minister of Agriculture said that he was sure the spirit of Saskatchewan was such that if a family was without flour some neighbour would come to the rescue. That is the spirit of Saskatchewan, of course; I think people in their poverty are more generous than people who are well to do. I have heard many remarkable stories of the extreme generosity of those who themselves have been in dire want. But the situation is that there are whole blocks of communities in which from 90 to 100 per cent of the people have been dependent upon government assistance for their supplies of food month by month. I am sure hon. members of this committee would have difficulty in grasping the meagreness of those supplies. I placed on the record previously some of the allowances that were made, and I am not going to repeat my statement to-night, but the conditions I described a year ago still prevail. Two or three weeks ago I was in my constituency for a few hours, and I saw two men who were leaving their wives and children because the government had notified them that no further relief would be given after May 31. These men were going to join the army, but I wish to tell this committee that they were not in the proper frame of mind to make their best contribution.
As I pointed out to the Minister of Agriculture, there are some things I think this country can do. We should be able to see that every home in Canada has all the flour that is necessary; and in a province like Saskatchewan, where they have had very little money spent in the development of war industries; where conditions are such that I think it will be extremely difficult for the provincial government to discharge its responsibilities to those people who are being reestablished, surely ways and means can be found to see that everyone has enough to eat. In the second place, I think the Minister of Labour should see that if these people are not going to be reestablished they should be given a chance to find some other employment. This government has been a party to taking these people from their homes in the southern part of the province-
No.
I understood that at the outset-
No; this act never applied to Saskatchewan.
But, as I understand it, this department has been guaranteeing a part of the money necessary to provide food for the people who were being reestablished. Is that not correct?
Yes; up to this year we have been supplying, direct relief.

The food the people
require in order to live is an important factor in that reestablishment. I do not kn,ow how those people are going to be able to survive because, as I have said, I do not see how the province of Saskatchewan can fulfil its responsibilities to them. If this government is not going to carry out the terms of the contract under which those people have been reestablished, then it is our duty to see that they are given a chance in industry. I know of some people being reestablished who were machinists and mechanics in the cities. They went north a few years ago to avoid going on relief or to get off relief, as they thought at that time. Some of them have been appealing to me to make contacts so that they may get back into industry in order to render some useful contribution in the present crisis. Some time ago the hon. member for Davenport told me that he never knew it to be so difficult to find employment for people in his riding; and there is not an hon. member who has offered me any encouragement to have people from my constituency come to Ontario or Quebec, or any other eastern province, in the hope that they may find employment. The Minister of Labour should do one of two things. He should either set up the necessary machinery to enable those people to find employment in those parts of Canada where industries are being operated, or continue to see that they have the wherewithal to obtain sufficient food in the meantime.

This relief settlement
project never did apply to Saskatchewan. It applied to Quebec, Manitoba and Alberta.

I do not know that the
hon. member who preceded the minister really referred to the reopening of direct relief. The more we see of this whole industrial and unemployment situation, the more we begin to realize how we have fallen down in connection with our national registration. Industries throughout Ontario are calling for mechanics to-day; and not only for mechanics but for labourers as well. I know a great many men who registered as having been machinists. I know men who were expert machinists at the time of the last war and who to-day are driving bread-wagons or doing other jobs not connected with war industry. We have men on the farms of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta who were formerly mechanics, but who to-day are in the position described by the hon. member for Mackenzie, of requiring relief.
The whole system of national registration has fallen down, because we have not taken advantage of it. If one talks to one minister of the government and says, something about industry, his reply is that this is the responsibility of some other minister. Minister after Minister will say, "This is not my responsibility; the Minister of Munitions and Supply will answer that." Another minister will say, "This is not my responsibility; the Minister of National Defence will answer that." There is not the coordination of effort in our war effort which we ought to have. The result is that if we had used national registration in the way we ought to have used it, we would have been in a position to choose the men who on their national registration cards said they could do this or that job. We could have moved them to those jobs.
Members of the government will reply that that is conscription of labour. I say that it is not conscription of labour. It is an allotment of labour to the jobs those people can do. The great difficulty has been lack of coordination among various departments of government, a failure to see to it that those who are on relief are moved to those sections of the country in which they could do something in our war effort, and earn an honest living without having to accept relief. In that way there would be coordination of our whole effort among the various departments, and we would be getting somewhere.
To-day some industries are being bogged down on account of the recruiting campaign. Industries are saying to departments of government, "Here are men we cannot spare;

here are men who are most important to our war effort." But because the government are anxious to see that the enlistment quota is filled before ninety days have expired, they are paying no attention to the necessity of retaining certain men in industry. On the other hand, there are a great many men in other parts of Canada who could be put into those industries, but to whom the government is paying no attention. My objection is that this lack of coordination among various departments of government is doing a great deal of harm to our whole war effort, and is making it necessary for members from various constituencies in western Canada to make appeals for the relief of their people.

The point of view of the government in respect of these matters is wrong. I have always been opposed to a system of direct relief. I believe that in 1931, when this procedure began, a most profound mistake was made. While the cost of public works may be greater, still the morale of the people is maintained by a public works programme. I certainly believe that if we have to face the situation again, we should never go in for a system of direct relief.
In the past few days in the House of Commons we have been speaking about recruiting and morale. I am of opinion that we are not going to maintain the morale of our people if we allow conditions to remain as they now exist in some parts of Saskatchewan, and in some of our larger cities. I read in the Montreal Gazette this morning that in that city there are 6,000 heads of families unemployed. If that condition continues, surely it offers no hope for the post-war period. As a matter of fact, it gives people the idea, "Well, we are going back to the same old conditions again, when this is all over."
At noon to-day I had the privilege of having lunch with a minister from a sister dominion, namely, New Zealand. He was describing the enthusiasm there was in that country. They have conscription for overseas service in New Zealand. But the main point is that they are not going to return to the kind of conditions to which our young men may have to return. Already they have organized wealth and industry, and they have compelled wealth to lend its money without interest to the state. They have given to the aged pensions at sixty, amounting to 30 shillings a week, or about $30 a month at the normal rate of exchange. They have free health services, hospitalization and maternity services.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Is that a contributory system?

Supply-Labour-Relief Commitments

Yes, a contributory
basis. Those factors maintain the morale of the people. Here to-night we are discussing unemployment relief. Of course, if we were manufacturing the commodities so badly needed overseas, we should have no unemployment in this country. But the fact is that we have unemployment; we have relief right at our doorsteps. I have said a number of times, and I shall say it to-night for the last time during this session, that if we wish to have the high morale we need in order to win the present conflict, we must plan for something better than the bread-line. We must see to it that during this war the people are fed and clothed and given an opportunity to work. I wish to impress that fact as forcibly as I can upon the minister and the government at this time.

One more thing we
must do: We must open our eyes and recognize the fact that when there are unemployed in Canada there are unemployed in Canada. We have not a shortage of labour. It is astounding to me that members of the administration and members of parliament generally will persist that we are short of men in Canada. Yet when we read the newspapers we find there are
6,000	unemployed in Montreal. How on earth people can possibly square the two situations, I do not know. We have enough labour and enough .unused resources to produce plenty of all the commodities Canada can produce for all her people, and still give to great Britain a great deal more than we are giving her. But we simply must reorganize our way of doing things so that we may bring together the labour, and the natural and financial resources of our country in order to achieve the desired end.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar):
That on Saturday, June 14, 1941, the house shall meet at eleven o'clock, and the order of business and procedure shall be the same as on Friday.
In making this motion, I desire to thank the committee for its cooperation to-night, and to offer also my thanks for anticipated cooperation to-morrow. I believe it is the general desire that the session be adjourned to-morrow. I do not speak for myself or for members of the government, because we live
in Ottawa, and it would not make much difference to us even if we sat next week. But it is the desire of hon. members generally, many of whom have already left, and others who have made arrangements to leave, that we should expedite business to-morrow in order to reach that end.
I wish to point out, however, that some time must be left for the hon. gentlemen of the other house in order that they-
